{Business and Leadership Conference} 
 {corner}  
{divider}

HDMA Members Respond to Nepal Earthquake

This weekend's devastating 7.8 magnitude earthquake in Nepal is the worst to hit the country in more than 80 years. Two of HDMA's allied service provider members — AmeriCares and Direct Relief International — are directly involved in the disaster relief efforts; their ability to respond is in part due to the commitment of our industry in partnering with them by providing supplies and financial support.

AmeriCares has been aiding survivors of natural disasters, political conflict and extreme poverty around the world for more than 30 years. An emergency response team from the AmeriCares' India office in Mumbai is headed to the impact zone and relief workers are preparing shipments of medical aid and relief supplies for survivors. Read more about the organization's efforts through the AmeriCares website. To donate to the organizations International Disaster Relief Fund, visit: americares.org/nepalearthquake.

Direct Relief International — a non-profit, non-partisan organization that provides medical assistance to people around the world who have been affected by poverty, natural disasters, and civil unrest — has made an initial cash commitment of $50,000 for the immediate deployment of emergency medical response personnel and essential health commodities, and has made available its entire current medical supply inventory, valued at $100 million, for the response. Find out more about the organization's Nepal earthquake response through its website.

The HDMA community has a long history of responding to emergencies; we are all united in our support for organizations like AmeriCares and Direct Relief International that are directly able to provide aid in times of crisis. For more information about HDMA's emergency preparedness and response efforts, visit www.HealthcareDistribution.org.

{top of page}

House Passes the Ensuring Patient Access and Effective Drug Enforcement Act of 2015

On April 25, the House of Representatives passed by voice vote the Ensuring Patient Access and Effective Drug Enforcement Act of 2015 (H.R. 471), sponsored by Reps. Marino (R-Pa.), Blackburn (R-Tenn.), Welch (D-Vt.) and Chu (D-Calif.) The bill was amended prior to passage to match the language under consideration in the Senate (S. 483) — sponsored by Sens. Hatch (R-Utah) and Whitehouse (D-R.I.).

"HDMA is pleased that the House of Representatives has once again passed this bipartisan legislation to help unite the pharmaceutical supply chain and regulators, such as the Drug Enforcement Administration, in their common goal of seeking to reduce prescription drug abuse and diversion," said HDMA President and CEO John M. Gray in a statement. "The nation's primary pharmaceutical distributors, through HDMA, now call on the Senate to take up [S. 483] in the hopes of promoting greater transparency in the fight against drug abuse and diversion."

The House bill was referred to the same committee of jurisdiction as the Senate companion, the Senate Judiciary Committee.

For more information, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.

{top of page}

FDA Guidance on "DSCSA Implementation: Product Tracing Requirement – Compliance Policy" Expires on May 1

HDMA's members are reminded that FDA's guidance, "DSCSA Implementation: Product Tracing Requirements – Compliance Policy" is set to expire on May 1.

The DSCSA had mandated that certain trading partners provide product information starting on January 1, 2015. The Compliance Policy detailed FDA's intention to not take enforcement action against trading partners that didnot provide product information as of January 1, as well as FDA's intention to exercise this enforcement discretion until May 1, 2015.

The enforcement discretion only applied to product tracing requirements and not to other requirements that went into effect on January 1, such as the notification of suspect products or the requirements regarding authorized trading partners.

View the December 31 announcement.

For more information, contact Anita Ducca or Allison Tuszynski.

{top of page}

Complete Your Business and Leadership Conference Appointment Requests by Friday, May 1

Attention Business and Leadership Conference meeting coordinators and table/team captains: time is running out to log into HDMA's appointment-scheduling software, PartnerLinx® 2.0, to request and rank your one-on-one-business appointments. The appointment request phase of the process will close this Friday, May 1. After this time, PartnerLinx will be closed to generate appointment schedules.

Visit the PartnerLinx website to manage your appointments. Your user name is your email address.

During the appointment request phase, distributors and manufacturers also may select service provider companies for appointments. Service providers are not able to request appointments in PartnerLinx, but are provided an attendee list so you can call on your trading partners to remind them to include your company in their selections. If you did not receive the attendee list, contact Lisa Gallagher for more information.

For appointment scheduling questions, contact Lisa Gallagher at (703) 885-0251.

For registration questions, contact HDMA's Meetings & Conferences Department at
(703) 885-0278.

{top of page}

Download HDMA's DSCSA Webinars

The recent webinars, "DSCSA Overview for Dispensers" and "Driving Toward DSCSA Implementation — Managing ASN Exceptions," are now available for download through the HDMA website.

"DSCSA Overview for Dispensers" highlighted the new requirements and DSCSA implementation timelines for dispensers, including what dispensers should expect in the coming year, how to better assess what to know, and tips on preparing internally and in partnership with supply chain trading partners. "Driving Toward DSCSA Implementation — Managing ASN Exceptions," provided an update on traceability implementation from a systems and technology perspective.

Both webinars were sponsored by Axway. For more information, contact Jo-Anne Torres, Manager, Education, at (703) 885-0273.

{top of page}

DEA Administrator Michelle Leonhart to Step Down in Mid-May

Michele Leonhart will step down in mid-May as the Administrator of the Drug Enforcement Administration. Leonhart became acting administrator in 2007 and has served as the Administrator since 2010. A recent inspector general report found that DEA agents engaged in inappropriate behavior funded by money taken from drug cartels. Subsequent to the publication of the report, several House Republican and Democratic members released a "no confidence" statement on Leonhart's capability as Administrator.

For more information, contact Anita Ducca or Allison Tuszynski.

{top of page}

House Subcommittee Will Host Third Hearing on Rx Drug Abuse on May 1

The House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations will hold a third hearing in its series on prescription drug abuse Friday, May 1 at 9:00 a.m. entitled, "What is the Federal Government Doing to Combat the Opioid Abuse Epidemic?" Witnesses and testimony will be posted on the committee website later this week.

The subcommittee held an April 23 hearing on "Combatting the Opioid Abuse Epidemic: Professional and Academic Perspectives." The hearing focused on treatment options for opioid addicts and best practices for those suffering from addiction and abuse. A witness list, testimony and additional information are available on the subcommittee website.

For more information, contact Jewelyn Cosgrove.

{top of page}

California Board of Pharmacy Releases Guidance for Third-Party Logistics Providers Currently Licensed as Drug Wholesalers

The California Board of Pharmacy recently released guidance for third-party logistics providers currently licensed as drug wholesalers. The guidance urges 3PLs currently licensed as wholesalers to immediately submit applications to become licensed as third-party logistics providers, or, if located outside California, as non-resident logistics providers.

California law does permit wholesalers and third-party logistics providers to be licensed in the same facility. However, each entity is required to have its own license, separate records and drug stock and different specially trained and licensed personnel (the responsible manager for the 3PL and a designated representative-in-charge for the wholesaler; designated representatives 3PL for the 3PL and designated representatives for the wholesaler).

Further information, including the Third-Party Logistics License Application and the Designated Representative (Individual) Third Party Logistics Licenses, is available on the Board of Pharmacy's website.

For more information, contact Liz Gallenagh.

Subject: FOR REVIEW: DRAFT EC EMAIL: Part D and Medicare Advantage 2019 Proposed Rule Released



 

The Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) released an advance copy of a proposed rule yesterday, proposing changes to Medicare Part D and Medicare Advantage (MA) plans for the 2019 contract year.  While we re still reviewing the rule, a few items to highlight include proposals such as:

 

 

           Manufacturer Rebates and Pharmacy Price Concessions to Point of Sale.  The proposed rule includes a Request for Information soliciting comments on potential policy approaches for applying some manufacturer rebates and all pharmacy price concessions to the price of a drug at the point of sale.  CMS states that they would use ideas and comments provided in response to the Request for Information to evaluate and consider proposals for rulemaking, but no proposals are currently included in the rule.  MNK Impact:  The idea of passing on rebates and other price concessions to consumers is being widely discussed, and would put pressure on Pharmacy Benefit Managers (PBMs) and insurers [KEVIN: we also may significant concessions/rebates to the distributors/wholesalers, so not aware if they re getting the same level of scrutiny as the PBMs, but they should be included], who may very likely oppose these ideas.  For patients, this could increase adherence and minimize patient abandonment rates and for pharmaceutical manufacturers, this would shine a brighter light on the ways in which PBMs and health plans utilize rebates and discounts. I would include whether MNK plans on commenting (I think we are, right? KEVIN: agree, we should comment) and whether we think this is neutral or positive or too soon to tell based on the information.

 

           Implementation of the Comprehensive Addiction and Recovery Act (CARA).  The proposal seeks to implement provisions of CARA by allowing Part D sponsors to establish a drug management program for  at risk beneficiaries.   Under such a program, Part D sponsors can limit access to frequently abused drugs, such as opioids, to a selected prescriber(s) and/or network pharmac(ies), sometimes also known as  lock in.   Specifically, Part D sponsors would be able to limit an at risk beneficiary s access to coverage of opioids beginning 2019 through a point-of-sale (POS) claim edit and/or by requiring the beneficiary to obtain opioids from a selected pharmacy(ies) and/or prescriber(s) after case management and notice to the beneficiary.  MNK Impact:  This will be an opportunity to highlight our view that opioids should be used sparingly, and that a balanced, multi-modal approach to pain management must be the preferred standard of care.  Restricting access to certain pharmacies or prescribers could negatively impact patient access to these medicines and negatively impact the specialty generics business. I would put this sentence first.[Kevin: Agree this should be first sentence.  What s not being said in the CMS document is what the sponsor is required to do if they limit access to medications. Our comments should state that the sponsor, if opioids are limited/withheld, would be required to provide the patient an alternative form of pain management, such as MMA]

 

           All opioids are proposed to be designated as  frequently abused drugs,  except for buprenorphine for medication-assisted treatment and injectables [Kevin: another example of CMS shifting market to buprenorphine and Vivitrol (injectable).  If they re going to call out MAT, they should say  all FDA approved MAT s].  MNK Impact:  Designating all opioids as  frequently abused  heightens the stigma around these medicine, and could be cause for concern.  Could also have a negative impact on MNK s methadone business.

 

           Mid-Year Formulary Changes.  Current regulations prohibit Part D sponsors and MA organizations from removing a covered Part D drug from a formulary or changing the preferred or tiered cost-sharing status of a covered Part D drug between the beginning of the annual election period and 60 days subsequent to the beginning of the contract year associated with that annual election period.  In the proposed rule, CMS would permit Part D sponsors to immediately remove brand name drugs (or to make changes in their preferred or tiered cost-sharing status), when those Part D sponsors replace the brand name drugs with (or add to their formularies) therapeutically equivalent newly approved generics--rather than having to wait until the direct notice and formulary change request requirements have been met.   MNK Impact:  Neutral.  The proposed mid-year formulary changes are concerning, as are proposals to change cost-sharing status for beneficiaries. This could cause patients to abandon medications if a change causes their cost sharing to increase mid-year.  If a therapeutically equivalent generic version of Acthar is approved in 2019, it could have a negative impact. Agree

 

           Any Willing Pharmacy Standard.  The proposed rule seeks to clarify Part D rules and CMS expectations regarding the statutorily required Any Willing Pharmacy provisions, and proposes to add a clarifying definition of mail-order pharmacy and revise the definition of retail pharmacy, among other changes.  Specifically, Part D sponsors are required to contract with any pharmacy that meets the Part D sponsor s standard terms and conditions for network participation.  In the proposed rule, CMS clarifies that the any willing pharmacy requirement applies to all pharmacies, regardless of how they have organized one or more lines of pharmacy business.  MNK Impact:  Neutral.  The proposed change would not apply to  at risk beneficiaries  and  frequently abused drugs  as described above.

 

           Biosimilar Payments.  CMS proposes to treat lower-cost  biosimilar  versions of biologic products like other generic drugs when determining how much certain beneficiaries pay for drugs out of pocket under Medicare Part D. This change seeks to encourage the availability of lower-cost alternatives for Medicare beneficiaries. MNK Impact:  Neutral.

 

The proposed rule is expected to be published on November 28, with comments due on January 8, 2018.  We will continue to review and engage with BIO and others as we prepare comments on behalf of MNK.

 

Please let us know if you have any questions.

{DEA Announces New Ways for the Public to Dispose of Unused Controlled Substances}DEA Announces New Ways for the Public to Dispose of Unused Controlled Substances

By Shannon O'Boye on September 8, 2014 Posted in Drug Policy

{Description: http://deachronicles.quarles.com/files/2014/09/Prescription_bottle_DEA_Blog-108x150.gif}Beginning next month, consumers will have an easier time getting rid of unused painkillers and other addictive drugs, which DEA hopes will discourage people from flushing the drugs down the toilet, throwing them in the garage, or leaving them, forgotten, in their medicine cabinets. The new disposal methods include allowing people to drop off unwanted pills at pharmacies, some hospitals and long-term care facilities, and police stations.

DEA s Final Rule, which implements the Secure and Responsible Drug Disposal Act of 2010 ( the Disposal Act ) by expanding the options to collect controlled substances back from ultimate users, is expected to be released tomorrow and will take effect on October 9. The disposal methods include take-back events, mail-back programs, and drop-off locations.

The new regulations:

allow authorized retail pharmacies; hospitals and clinics with on-site pharmacies; manufacturers; distributors; reverse distributors; and narcotic treatment programs (NTPs), to place collection receptacles inside their establishments and to permit people to mail back unwanted controlled substance mediations;
expand the authority of authorized pharmacies and hospitals/clinics to place collection receptacles inside long-term care facilities; and
allow law enforcement agencies to place collection receptacles inside their stations, conduct drug take-back events, and administer mail-back programs. (Note that law enforcement agencies are not required to use collection receptacles that meet all of the specifications in the rule.)

DEA registrants that want to become controlled substances  collectors  will need authorization from the Agency to keep secure containers at their locations for controlled substances drop off or to conduct mail-back programs. A registrant may seek to modify its DEA registration to become a collector by making a written request by mail or online. Retail pharmacies and hospitals/clinics that become collectors will be allowed to put collection receptacles inside long-term care facilities for those facilities  residents.

For security reasons, collection receptacles must be securely fastened to a permanent structure. In addition, as a general rule, the collection receptacles must be placed in the immediate proximity of a designated area where controlled substances are stored and where an employee is present. Hospitals/clinics, which would have difficulty meeting that requirement, must place receptacles in locations that are regularly monitored by employees and are not in the proximity of any area where emergency or urgent care is provided.

Collection receptacles must be accessible to the public because only the ultimate users of the drugs are authorized to place the controlled substances in a receptacle. Pharmacy and hospital staff cannot take the drugs and put them into a container.

Registrants that choose to conduct mail-back programs must be able to destroy returned packages on site. And registrants must provide customers with mail-back packages. They can charge for the packaging, or provide the packaging for free.

The new rule permits controlled substances collected through take-back events, mail-back programs, and collection receptacles to be comingled with non-controlled substances.

Other highlights of the Rule:

Methods of Destruction:

DEA is not requiring a specific method of destruction for controlled substances that are collected. Registrants are free to develop their own methods of destruction so long as, in the end, the drug is  non-retrievable , which means the condition or state to which a controlled substance must be rendered following a process that permanently alters the controlled substance s physical or chemical condition or state through irreversible means and thereby renders the controlled substance unavailable and unusable for all practical purposes. See 21 C.F.R.   1300.05(b). Once a controlled substance is  non-retrievable,  it is not longer subject to DEA requirements.

Long-Term Care Facilities:

In addition to allowing retail pharmacies and hospitals/clinics with on-site pharmacies to place collection receptacles in LTCFs for residents, DEA is also implementing special security requirements for these collection receptacles to encourage their use.

First, DEA is permitting sealed inner liners that have been removed from collection receptacles to be stored at LTCFs for up to three business days in a securely-locked, substantially constructed cabinet or in a securely-locked room with controlled access until the liners can be transferred for destruction. However, DEA is encouraging authorized collectors to schedule inner liner removals on the same day that medications are delivered, if possible, to make storage of sealed inner liners unnecessary.

It is also important to note that collectors cannot transfer sealed inner liners from LTCFs to their registered locations (i.e., the pharmacy or hospital/clinic). DEA is concerned that pharmacy or hospital/clinic employees transporting large quantities of controlled substances pose a security risk. Therefore, collectors must deliver sealed inner liners to a reverse distributor or a distributor by common or contract carrier or by reverse distributor or distributor pick-up at the LTCF.

Second, collectors will be allowed to have one of its employees and a supervisory level employee of the LTCF (e.g., a charge nurse, supervisor, or similar employee) install, remove, store, or transfer inner liners, or the collector can have two of its own employees do the work.

DEA hopes that these modifications will result in expanded safe and secure disposal options for LTCF residents.

DEA Registrant Disposal:

DEA has modified DEA Form 41 and is requiring that the form to be used to record the destruction of controlled substances that remain in the closed system of distribution and to account for the destruction of controlled substances collected from consumers and other non-registrants pursuant to the Disposal Act.

Reverse Distributors:

DEA added a definition of  reverse distribute,  revised the definition of  reverse distributor , and clarified that the security, inventory, and recordkeeping requirements for controlled substance destruction apply to some entities that reverse distribute even if they are not required to register as reverse distributors.

In addition, DEA has extended the time that a registrant that reverse distributes has to destroy controlled substances to 30 days, from the proposed 14 days.

Distributors may acquire controlled substances from collectors for the purpose of destruction, as a coincident activity to distribution.

The rules are intended to expand the options available to safely and securely dispose of potentially dangerous prescription medications on a routine basis. Beginning in 2010, DEA has sponsored eight National Prescription Drug Take-Back events around the country that resulted in the collection of more than 4.1 millions pounds (over 2,100 tons) of medication at over 6,000 locations.

text:
Subject: Exalgo mentioned by Dr. Webster in Medscape article
From: "Littlejohn, Stephen E" <stephen.littlejohn@covidien.com>
Date: Thu, 05 Apr 2012 16:18:01 -0500
To: "Bozzini, Alfredo" <alfredo.bozzini@covidien.com>,
    "Patrick, Jeffrey" <jeffrey.patrick@covidien.com>,
    "Saake, Lisa M" <lisa.saake@covidien.com>,
    "Harrell, Jamie" <jamie.harrell@covidien.com>,
    "Terifay, Terry W" <terry.terifay@covidien.com>,
    "Novak, Rod P" <rod.novak@covidien.com>,
    "Wessler, Michael" <michael.wessler@covidien.com>,
    "Brendel, Diane" <diane.brendel@covidien.com>




Opioid Rotation Practices Linked to Fatalities
Pauline Anderson
April 5, 2012 - Opioid rotation - switching from one opioid drug or route of administration to another to improve the outcome - is largely to blame for the growing number of unintentional deaths related to opioids, a new review suggests.
The review cites evidence of a link between opioid-related deaths and common opioid rotation practices, including the use of dose-conversion ratios published in equianalgesic tables.
Opioid rotation is flawed, said study coauthor Lynn R. Webster, MD, president elect of the American Academy of Pain Medicine and medical director and founder of Lifetree Clinical Research, Salt Lake City, Utah. Although using conversion tables is harmless in most cases, "this is an area where the harm has such devastating consequences - death - that we cannot accept even a 1% error," said Dr. Webster.
Along with his coauthor, Perry G. Fine, MD, Pain Research Center and Pain Management Center, University of Utah, Salt Lake City, Dr. Webster reviewed the literature and found several case reports of opioid-related deaths or "near misses."
The review was published online<http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1526-4637.2012.01357.x/abstract> March 28 in Pain Medicine, the official journal of the American Academy of Pain Medicine.
In an accompanying article<http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1526-4637.2012.01356.x/abstract> published at the same time in the same journal, Dr. Webster and Dr. Fine suggest a slower and potentially safer method for switching opioids.
Painkiller Overdoses
Almost 15,000 people die every year as a result of overdoses involving prescription painkillers, with that number exceeding deaths from heroine and cocaine combined, according to a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention<http://www.medscape.com/viewarticle/752700> report. The US Food and Drug Administration<http://archinte.ama-assn.org/cgi/content/abstract/167/16/1752> (FDA) found that opioids, including oxycodone, fentanyl, morphine, methadone, and acetaminophen/hydrocodone, accounted for 5 of the 15 drugs most frequently named in fatal outcomes.
According to the new review, most proposed protocols for opioid rotation involve the use of equianalgesic dosing tables to convert the dose of the original opioid to a putative equivalent dose of morphine. That dose is then converted to that for the new opioid, with a safety margin incorporated.
One of the problems is that the most widely accepted guideline for opioid rotation was developed many years ago. At the time, experts believed that the relative strength of one opioid compared with that of another in the chronic state would be the same as that in the acute state, said Dr. Webster. "In other words, we didn't take into account that people would develop a tolerance, and certainly until just recently, we never knew about the genetic issues."
Not only did most studies use a single dose or a limited range of doses, they also investigated only a specific route. Thus, the findings aren't generalizable to other routes. Further, the studies didn't account for responses based on ethnicity, advanced age, concomitant medication use, or comorbid conditions.
"The key issue is that every human being has a different sensitivity to every different opioid molecule," said Dr. Webster. "So the way you respond to morphine will be different to the way that I respond to morphine, even in the acute state."
The rotation protocol has never been formally validated for safety or efficacy, added Dr. Webster. "There has never been an attempt to determine what is an equal analgesic of 1 opioid over another for chronic use - for example, after someone has been on a drug for 6 months or a year or 2. There is no research that has demonstrated consistently, across the board, that these tables have any validity."
Relying on tables derived from single-dose studies is especially problematic with repeated dosing of methadone. The authors noted the FDA's public health advisory on deaths and life-threatening changes in breathing and heart rate in patients newly started on methadone.
Although prescribing a new pain reliever might be necessary because of loss of effectiveness or side effects, in many cases the switch is called for because an insurer no longer covers a particular drug, said Dr. Webster. "So doctors have been forced to move to less costly drugs, and the least costly is usually methadone."
Gambling With Life?
Contributing to the problem is that published equianalgesic tables have inconsistent and variable conversion ratios. In addition, dose conversion guidelines found in package inserts for opioids, particularly the newer extended-release opioids, are inconsistent and potentially dangerous, said Dr. Webster.
He used the example of hydromorphone (Exalgo, Mallinckrodt/Covidien); the language of the insert is such that the conversion would result in 1 of 3 options, he said: an underestimate of the amount of extended-release hydromorphone necessary for adequate analgesia, an overestimate of the necessary amount that could increase the risk for overdose, or a dose within a reasonable window.
This, said Dr. Webster, boils down to "guessing" or "gambling" on the part of the clinician. "When we're dealing with a life, we should not be gambling."
Prescribing competence is "shockingly inadequate," said the authors. Errors can stem from inadequate education, lack of attention to detail, and calculation errors.
Confusion can also contribute to the problem. A survey of 406 non-pain specialist physicians found that 59% had difficulty calculating opioid dosages when rotating. When asked to convert a daily dose of 60 mg oxycodone to the dose for a fentanyl patch, 41% of clinical specialists, 28% of general practitioners, and 17% of geriatric care physicians said they "don't know" how to do that.
Physicians may be lulled into believing that conversion tables are safe and appropriate. "We like to have things structured in medicine," said Dr. Webster. "These tables were established to some degree to provide some security and safety and guidance toward rotating, but the irony is that they've actually made it unsafe."
Research suggests that 50% to 80% of patients with chronic pain who respond poorly to one opioid improve after being rotated to another opioid.
In their second report, a clinical case also published in Pain Medicine, Dr. Webster and Dr. Fine suggest an alternative to using opioid-rotation tables.
The best approach, they suggest, is to decrease the first drug by 25% to 30% per week while introducing the new drug at a dose that would be given to an opioid-naive patient, increasing the dose according to the clinical response, said Dr. Webster. "In many instances, it may take 3 to 4 weeks to rotate from one opioid to another," he said.
If patients are experiencing pain during the switch, physicians should give an immediate-release opioid to help "bridge" inadequate dosing.
He cautioned that some patients may be sensitive to the new drug. "A new molecule may be highly effective at a very low dose."
Hold Next Dose
Seddon Savage, MD, medical director, Chronic Pain and Addiction Program, Silver Hill Hospital, New Canaan, Connecticut, and president of the American Pain Society, agrees with this slow rotation protocol.
She added that patients should be told that if they feel sedated they should hold their next opioid dose and call their physician.
Dr. Savage commented that the review paper does a good job of pointing out and documenting the problems related to opioid rotation and of making physicians more aware of the limitations of conversion tables.
"One of the points that the authors make is that there is a lot of variability in response to different opioids. If you take these opioid conversion tables as gospel, apply them indiscriminately to all people, and just do a mathematical conversion, you will end up with some people for whom the conversion aren't appropriate."
For a list of companies from which Dr. Webster has received funding, and for conflict of disclosures for Dr. Fine, please see original paper.
Pain Medicine. Both articles published online March 28, 2012. Abstract<http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1526-4637.2012.01357.x/abstract> Abstract<http://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1111/j.1526-4637.2012.01356.x/abstract>

Dear all:

» Driving in this morning heard a lengthy piece on NPR by Laura Sullivan, Washington correspondent on
Zohydro and petitions currently running to get FDA to withdraw approval of the drug.
»

Diane can you speak to GreenRoom and get a transcript ASAP?

Needs to go to everyone on this message.

» Mario we need your help with a couple of additional follow ons....we need to develop an answer to a
question that is basically, "Why aren't the risks "to public health" with XXR the same as zohydro?" Two
overarching messages of the piece were about the big opioid payload of zohydro and the ease with which
the tablet can be crushed. Without making head to head comparisons, we can state info about the two
components of XXR and the size of the opioid component. But what will be able to say in answer to a
direct question about, " Can XXR be easily crushed?"
» Marily, Bill and DC folks, please also develop a rough list of the "public health groups" that are
said to be pressuring FDA for Zohydro withdrawal . I think we want to consider a post-approval outreach
to give at least some of them direct information on XXR. I'm not signing up to that yet, but we need to
think about who they are, who we may know in leadership of the most vocal groups, how they may be tied
(or not) to the AG efforts, and what an approach might look like. I don't want to over play this and
call attention where none would naturally be, but I also think that ignorance of how XXR is different
than Zohydro is our enemy. On balance we may need to take the risk of educating some NGOs in order to
lower overall risk/noise in the market. Please start the background work and we can discuss it with
Hugh, Mario and Others next week.
» re

Subject: EXALGO Mini Modules Proposal
From: Vince Mevoli <vmevoli@synchronyhc.com>
Date: Mon, 09 Apr 2012 17:31:25 -0500
To: "Falcone, Melissa M" <melissa.falcone@covidien.com>


Hi Melissa:


Hope all's well.


Sorry for the delay in getting this over to you, but attached is a proposal for the development of three "mini modules".  I know that we did not get the chance to talk through our thoughts in more detail before developing the proposal, but we made some assumptions regarding what the new topics should be, as well as the specifications for finalizing each deck.  This includes two new cases   one focused on an Opana ER patient, and one focused on a Duragesic patch patient.  The third topic will highlight the first week on Exalgo, and will go into more detail about what to expect regarding conversion, initiation, and titration, including key points to help set patient expectations during that time.  


Each mini module would consist of about 25 total slides, including a required set of core slides (eg, boxed warning, IRI, other core brand message slides), about 5 de novo slides w/notes, and 5 slides/notes that will be based on approved slide content but will be modified as necessary to better tell the story in the context of the new deck.New and modified slide content could include, but is not limited to, new case study slides, a focus on patients taking SSRIs and the potential impact on drug/drug interactions, expanding rescue medication usage from clinical trials, more in-depth content on dose proportionality, and creating a one-slide overview of the CAT (Calculate, Adjust, Titrate) approach to treatment.


Let me know once you've had the chance to review the attached proposal, and we can  can set up some time address any questions/thoughts you may have and discuss next steps.

Memorandum 
 
To:           David Moody 
 
CC:          Jim Meyer; Hal Harrison 
 
From:     Tom Readling 
 
Date:      6/9/2009 
 
Re:          Receipt of Tampered Shipment: Mallinckdrot Oxycodone W/APAP 7.5/325 mg 
 
On Monday, June 8, 2009 at approximately 11:00 AM a shipment was received from Mallinckrodt via FedEx. The shipment was signed for and the driver released before the shipment was checked. 
 
The items were delivered in a cardboard box which had been secured with strapping tape. The contents of the box were shrink wrapped in blue plastic.  
 
Gene Thompson checked the shipment in, which included 82 cases of Oxycodone w/apap 10/325 in 100 count bottles (SKU 609-826) and 11 cases of oxycodone w/apap 7.5/325 mg in 100 count bottles (SKU 609-842). During the process Thompson noticed one of the cases of the Oxycodone w/apap 7.5/325 mg had been opened and was missing three (3) bottles. The case in question contained nine (9) bottles instead of the usual twelve (12).  
 
Thompson notified David Thompson who in turn contacted writer. Writer observed the box and noted that the tape securing the box appeared to have been cut and the case was missing three bottles. The case was subsequently photographed by Phuong Ho and the photographs will be maintained. 
 
The shipment noted above was order number 7726533, PO# S48986, and the FedEx tracking number was 9864 7326 9667. The FedEx shipment was made 2-day freight and appears to have originated in Hobart, NY. 
 
Individuals in receiving have indicated that it is FedEx policy that a Mutual employee must sign for the shipment before it can be opened. The driver will subsequently note any problems with the shipment. 
 
The associates in receiving have been instructed to inspect all shipments received from FedEx and to ask for assistance if the inspection requires it. The driver from FedEx is to remain until the shipment has been inspected for tampering.

Some good news from FDA for the planned Exalgo labeling changes.  FDA has agreed that we may submit the safety labeling changes as CBE-0 based on the updated Jurnista CCDS.  The safety labeling documents should be available this week for submission prior to the end of March.

Subject:DEA Suspicious Order Quantities
I wanted to advise all of you that we re working with Security and the DEA Compliance  Group (Bill Ratliff
and Karen Harper) to develop procedures to insure we maintain compliance with the DEA  requirement
that we report any suspicious order quantities and/or patterns to them. In light of  the recent
developments with McKesson, a good deal of focus is being placed on this project.
Briefly, if an order is deemed  peculiar  by a customer service rep based on a set of  guidelines currently
being developed, it will be placed on hold and the DEA compliance group (Bill Ratliff  and Karen Harper)
will be advised. DEA Compliance will then conduct a more in-depth investigation and determine if the
situation warrants notification to the DEA. If the order is deemed appropriate, customer service will be
notified and the order will be released from hold status for shipment. If the outcome of the investigation
supports that the order is in fact  suspicious  it will not be shipped and the local  DEA office will be notified.
 I would expect that we also develop a means of communication to the business group any time an order
is placed on hold for reasons of peculiarity by the Customer Service Group. Updates  regarding the status
of specific orders should be forwarded as well as the  peculiar order  proceeds through the review process.
Preliminary processes are in development and I m in the process of determining/evaluating how best to
identify deviations from the norm based on the type of businesses we service as well as the products being
purchased. Criteria that is well suited for an AT Clinic may be too stringent for a Distributor. Each class of
customer (clinics, distributors, wholesalers, etc.) will be handled based on the merits of the business
segment they support. Any anomalies that support what we term as a  peculiar  order will be forwarded
to the DEA compliance group for further investigation prior to it being turned over to the DEA.
As these respective formulas are developed, I will share them with you along with a sampling of data used
to support the validity/effectiveness of the assumptions used in developing same. At first pass, the
formula might look like this:
- Customers will be separated into their respective class of business (distributors, wholesalers, clinic, hospitals,
retail, etc)
- Add purchase quantities, by product (all Oxy products and again by individual skus) for the last 12 months
for all customers within the same class of business for any controlled substances
o  Customer s with multiple  ship to  locations should have their total aggregated at the  sold to  level;
but also reviewed at the  ship to  level
- Add customer months for every record used in the above total (months within the last 12 that customer
purchases of the item were not zero)
- Divide total quantity purchases by the total customer months
- Then multiply by the factor below to give the maximum mount that the customer can order per month
before showing up on the suspicious order report.
o  Factor = 2 for C-II Controlled Substances
o  Factor = 4 for C-III, IV and V
Once the myriad aspects of this project are refined, selective excess order quantity business rules may


   require adjustment.
In addition to order quantities by product, we hope to also develop criteria for orders that deviate from
normal ordering patterns and/or from usual order frequency (not yet sure how to capture this; hope to
identify an algorithm that will support parsing through the data to identify patterns, frequency, etc.) A
report will be generated daily (at a minimum) but hope to eventually have the systems  in place so
customer service receives a  real time  flag when an order violates one of our parameters and will flag the
order as peculiar.
The group is working on other indicators that might be used in evaluating whether or not a customer
should be reported as  peculiar . The Sales force will play a key role in this process by verifying the
customer s physical site and operations ring true with the type of business they purport to run. The DEA
Compliance group is in the process of discussing this aspect with management on the Sales side of the
business.
If you have any questions, please let me know. This process is in preliminary stages  so we may not have
answers to all the questions that may come up, but those questions might also be food  for thought in
furthering the breadth of this project.
Regards,

Subject: Alert: Health Care Policy Report: Highlights
From: Bloomberg Government <alerts@bgov.com>
Date: Fri, 13 Oct 2017 16:15:53 +0000
To: derek.naten@mallinckrodt.com


{Bloomberg Government}  

 

 

Health Care Policy Report: Highlights

October 13, 2017 12:15PM ET | Bloomberg BNA


 

 

 

 

The following is the latest issue of the Bloomberg BNA Health Care Policy Reports:

HIGHLIGHTS AND CONTENTS

1. Trump Threatens Obamacare Chaos as He Cuts Off Insurer Subsidy

President Donald Trump's administration took its most drastic step yet to roll back the Affordable Care Act on the evening of Oct. 12, cutting off a subsidy to insurers just hours after issuing an executive order designed to draw people away from the health law's coverage markets. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

2. Democrats Skeptical of New Children's Health Deal

Republicans aren't willing to change significant details of their bill extending funding for the Children's Health Insurance Program, which is likely to kill chances Democrats will support it, Rep. Frank Pallone Jr. (D-N.J.) told Bloomberg BNA Oct. 11. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

3. Trump Moves to Undo Obamacare After Repeal Drive Fails on Hill

President Donald Trump began his own effort to undo major parts of the Affordable Care Act, after Republican leaders in Congress failed to repeal and replace his predecessor's signature legislative accomplishment. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

4. GOP Lawmaker Calls for Transparency in Drug Discount Program

Congress must ensure accountability and transparency in the federal 340B drug discount program, Rep. Morgan Griffith (R-Va.) said Oct. 11. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

5. Trump Cuts to Obamacare Enrollment Groups Deeper Than Expected

The Trump administration is cutting tens of millions of dollars from organizations that help Americans enroll in Obamacare health plans, leaving some of the groups scrambling to shrink their operations weeks before enrollment for 2018 coverage opens on Nov. 1. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

6. Democrats Seek Relaxed Medicaid Rules for Hurricane Victims

Federal authorities should relax Medicaid eligibility rules for those affected by hurricanes in Puerto Rico and the U.S. Virgin Islands, House Democrats told the Trump administration. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

7. Puerto Rico Medicaid Funding in Spotlight After Hurricane

The House Energy and Commerce Committee passed in a divided vote $1 billion in additional funding for Puerto Rico's Medicaid program as part of its bill reauthorizing the lapsed Children's Health Insurance Program. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

8. House Approves Federal Diabetes Panel

Health officials would create a new panel to coordinate the federal response to diabetes and related illnesses under a bill passed by the House Oct. 11. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

9. What GOP Budget Means for Health Care

Republicans say they'll keep their tax reform and Obamacare overhaul plans separate, but Democrats are warning that the GOP left the door open for changes to the health law as well as to Medicare and Medicaid. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

10. Groups, States Oppose HHS Change to Birth Control Mandate

Opposition to Trump administration changes to rules implementing Obamacare's birth control coverage requirement is moving into court. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

11. Many Ideas, Little Consensus in House on Opioid Epidemic

There appears to be little consensus among House lawmakers about how Congress should respond to the opioid epidemic. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

12. Trump Names Hargan as Acting Health and Human Services Secretary

President Donald Trump has formally designated Eric Hargan as acting secretary of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services, taking over for a deputy who's held the job since Tom Price resigned from the post late last month over his use of taxpayer dollars to travel in private jets. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

13. Trump Slows Efforts to Cut Health-Care Costs

In April 2016 the federal Medicare program began an experiment to save money on the half-million hip and knee replacements it pays for each year. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

14. Obamacare Would Be Further Weakened by Trump Order, Experts Say

An executive order from President Donald Trump to allow new health plans outside of Obamacare could further destabilize the law's fragile markets, health-care experts say. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

15. Almost Half of Medicare Managed Care Plans Get Top Ratings

Close to half (44 percent) of Medicare managed care plans that combine health services and the Part D drug benefit are rated at least four stars on a one-to-five scale for the 2018 plan year, the Medicare agency said Oct. 11. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

16. Medicare Panel Wants Congress to Scrap Doctor Reporting Program

Congress's Medicare advisers Oct. 5 appeared close to recommending that the nine-month-old physician quality reporting system be killed. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

17. Extend Relaxed Medicare Doc Pay Rules, Groups Tell Congress

Congress should allow Medicare to continue slowing down implementation of certain provisions of the new doctor quality payment program for three more years, the American Medical Association and 114 medical groups said. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

18. Medicare Panel Urges Caution on Telehealth Expansion

Congress's Medicare advisers are concerned it may be premature to expand telehealth coverage. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

19. GOP Senators Push for Vote on 20-Week Abortion Ban

Several Senate Republicans Oct. 5 called for a vote on a House-passed ban on abortions after 20 weeks of pregnancy. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

20. Senator Demands OPM Explain Treatment of Congress Under ACA

The Office of Personnel Management is being asked to produce, by Oct. 18, all of the information it has regarding the Obama-era decision to allow members of Congress and their staffs to get special consideration, including an employer contribution, for their health plans under the Affordable Care Act. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

21. Trump Order on Health Insurance Sales Across State Lines Delayed

An executive order from President Donald Trump boosting sales of health insurance across state lines has been delayed, according to people following the issue. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

22. California Laws Protect Obamacare from Federal Threats

Gov. Jerry Brown (D) signed bills Oct. 4 to prop up California's embrace of the Affordable Care Act in the face of federal changes. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

23. Federal Subsidy Uncertainty Means Calif. Obamacare Hike

California's health benefits exchange is tacking an average 12.4 percent surcharge on some plans in 2018 to minimize the uncertainty of federal cost-sharing subsidies from the Trump administration. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

24. Nevada Legislature Intervenes in Drug-Pricing Lawsuit

The Nevada Legislature is stepping in to defend a new drug-pricing law that industry groups say violates the U.S. Constitution. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

25. Will Storm-Struck Nursing Home Find Shelter From Litigation?

Families suing a Florida nursing home over its post-hurricane evacuation and more than a dozen deaths will have to work around state laws that attorneys say shelter the industry from large damages awards. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

26. Planned Parenthood, ACLU Team Up to Take on Missouri Abortion Law

A Missouri law set to take effect Oct. 24 that places additional restrictions on legal abortion is invalid, two abortion rights groups claim. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

27. Pennsylvania Joins States With Drug, Device Right-to-Try Laws

Terminally ill patients in Pennsylvania will have the right to try experimental treatments under legislation Gov. Tom Wolf (D) signed into law Oct. 11. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

28. West Virginia to Use Medicaid for Substance Abuse Treatment

West Virginia, which has the highest rate of drug overdose deaths in the country, will become the fifth state to use Medicaid dollars to battle substance abuse. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

29. Union Alleges Seattle-Area Health System Fails Charity Duty

An organized-labor backed report released Oct. 10 accuses CHI Franciscan Health, a metropolitan Seattle health-care system, of failing to follow its legal and moral obligations to provide charity care. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

30. Tennessee Doctors Say Payment Reform Effort Flawed

Tennessee's episodes-of-care incentive payment program is flawed and unfair and not working for physicians, a representative of state providers says. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

31. Physicians Leading Campaign for Alaska Insurance Provisions

A group of Alaska doctors is offering two ballot initiatives that would establish several popular features of the Affordable Care Act as statewide insurance requirements. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

32. Drug Profits Catch Wall Street's Eye in Flurry of FDA Approvals

Gridlock under the Trump administration, particularly the repeated failures to repeal and replace Obamacare, is riveting the nation's attention. Yet at least one government agency is running smoothly—and even accelerating its operations. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

33. Drugmakers Face Puerto Rico Factory Challenges as Storm Passes

Drugmakers rode out Hurricane Maria in Puerto Rico, but keeping plants running while the devastated island picks up the pieces is likely to be tougher. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

34. Express Scripts to Buy Medical Gatekeeper for $3.6 Billion

Express Scripts Holding Co. agreed to pay $3.6 billion to acquire closely held EviCore Healthcare, a company that preapproves scans and other costly medical tests for health plans. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

35. Amazon Looms Over Pharmacy Chains as Analysts See Market Entry

Amazon.com Inc. is almost certain to enter the business of selling prescription drugs by 2019, said two analysts at Leerink Partners, posing a direct threat to the U.S.’s biggest brick-and-mortar drugstore chains. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

36. Disaster Preparedness Essentials for Healthcare Facilities

Natural disasters cause nearly 500 deaths annually in the United States. Unfortunately, healthcare facilities in the U.S. continue to fall short in disaster planning and preparedness. This lack of preparation creates the potential for serious ramifications, putting staff, patients, and the financial security of the hospital at risk. Below are five key components to an effective emergency management plan. {Link to Story}(Story Link)

Subject: Good Morning


To all

I hope that each of you had a tremendous week and are prepared to recharge this weekend. As I am sitting in the Dublin Airport awaiting my flight back home, I thought it would be beneficial to recap the Strategic Plan Board presentation:

1. The overall feedback from the board was complimentary on not only the aspiration of our plan but also the amount of progress we have made over our last twelve months.

2. There was robust conversation regarding the future expansion of the business beyond Questcor and ultimately there was agreement about the potential external opportunities necessary to deliver the plan.

3. A large degree of time was dedicated to capabilities throughout the organization. While there was recognition of the positive steps we have made as a company, the challenge ahead for all of us is to be extremely rigorous in our approach to building the capabilities required for us to be successful now and throughout the plan. This will require us to be courageous in our approach to performance management in order to ensure that our teams reach their full potential while upgrading talent where appropriate.

4. As it relates to the commercial review, the Board was supportive of the plan but challenged me to ensure that we are realistic and prepared in our responses to the needs of the market. As you recall, the US Spec Pharma plan delivers a 10% CAGR on the top line and a 12% CAGR on the bottom line across the entire 5 year landing period. To deliver these results will require the commercial team to embrace the idea of continuos improvement across all facets of our organization. We cannot allow ourselves to be content with our current skills and capabilities. We have to build customer intimacy in order to ensure impact and value for our teams. We must build the voice of the customer into our plans earlier in the process while challenging our assumptions of what will be necessary to succeed. Finally, we have to embrace the business acumen required to ensure our investments deliver the required return for the company.

5. Finally, the Board confirmed what we have been saying all along, this plan will require Mallinckrodt to become a Commercial Excellent organization. All facets of the broader company must be focused on what will be required to win in the marketplace. It was clear to the Board as it has been to us, the future of Mallinckrodt lies squarely in the hands of the commercial organization.

I couldn't be more thankful to each of you for the amount of dedication and effort that you bring to your job everyday. Leadership is not easy and it requires not only vision but also collaboration and trust. It is up to each of us to work together, to let go of whatever personal agendas might exist and focus on the greater good of the organization. We must learn to work together, to push each other, to trust each other and finally, to support each other. These are the characteristics of great teams.

There is no doubt that we have our work cut for us, including:

1. The stabilization and return to growth for Ofirmev
2. The correction of the Xartemis XR launch curve
3. Improving the effectiveness and impact of our customer facing teams
4. Building our commercial excellence capabilities
5. Continuing to feed the growth of our multi source business through both internal and external opportunities
6. Successfully preparing the market and the launch of MNK-155
7. Strengthening our Market Access presence and impact for the entire portfolio
8. Integrating Acthar Gel and other external opportunities as they occur

This team has the chance to deliver the future for Mallinckrodt. I hope that each of you are excited as I am about this rare opportunity.

Thanks and have a great weekend. I will be in NJ moving next week but I will be available by phone, text or email so please don't hesitate to reach out.

All the best

Hugh

Mallinckrodt Announces Agreement with Xanodyne to Purchase Roxicodone?

  HAZELWOOD, MO ? August 23, 2012 ? Mallinckrodt, the Pharmaceuticals business of Covidien (NYSE: COV), today announced that it has entered into an agreement with Xanodyne Pharmaceuticals to purchase Roxicodone? (oxycodone hydrochloride tablets USP) in 5, 15 and 30 mg dosage strengths. Roxicodone, currently marketed in the United States, is an immediate release formulation of oxycodone indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain where the use of an opioid analgesic is appropriate. With this agreement, Mallinckrodt acquires all rights to the Roxicodone New Drug Application (NDA).  No financial details were disclosed. 

 

"We are excited about this agreement as it complements our existing portfolio of opioids and leverages our pain management expertise,? said Mark Trudeau, President, Pharmaceuticals. ?More importantly, we are committed to safe and effective use of all of our products along with ensuring access for all patients in need of pain treatment.?

  Mallinckrodt is the largest U.S. supplier of opioid pain medications and among the top 10 generic pharmaceuticals manufacturers in the U.S., based on prescriptions.  Its branded portfolio includes EXALGO? (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) and PENNSAID? (diclofenac sodium topical solution) 1.5% w/w.  Mallinckrodt is also one of the world?s leading producers of bulk acetaminophen.

  Covidien announced last December that the Company planned to spin off Mallinckrodt into a stand-alone company, a process that is expected to be completed in mid-2013.

   IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION

  About ROXICODONE

  Roxicodone tablets are contraindicated in patients with known hypersensitivity to oxycodone, or in any situation where opioids are contraindicated. This includes patients with significant respiratory depression (in unmonitored settings or the absence of resuscitative equipment) and patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma or hypercarbia. Oxycodone hydrochloride tablets are contraindicated in any patient who has or is suspected of having paralytic ileus.

  Serious adverse reactions that may be associated with Roxicodone tablets therapy include: respiratory depression, respiratory arrest, circulatory depression, cardiac arrest, hypotension, and/or shock.  Common adverse events that may be associated with Roxicodone tablets therapy include:  nausea, constipation, vomiting, headache, pruritus, insomnia, dizziness, asthenia, and somnolence.

  About EXALGO

  INDICATION

  EXALGO? (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

  WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL, LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION,
and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE

Abuse Potential

  EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient?s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.

  Life-threatening Respiratory Depression

  Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.

  Accidental Exposure

  Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.


  ?         EXALGO is contraindicated in:

-   Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.

-   Patients with significant respiratory depression

-   Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or in the absence of resuscitative equipment

-   Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus

-   Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the gastrointestinal tract, or have ?blind loops? of the gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction

-   Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications

  ?         Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.

  
  About PENNSAID

PENNSAID is a nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (?NSAID?) indicated for the treatment of signs and symptoms of osteoarthritis of the knee(s).

<?XML:NAMESPACE PREFIX = V /> 
WARNING: CARDIOVASCULAR AND GASTROINTESTINAL RISK

Cardiovascular Risk

? Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) may cause an increased risk of serious cardiovascular thrombotic events, myocardial infarction, and stroke, which can be fatal. This risk may increase with duration of use. Patients with cardiovascular disease or risk factors for cardiovascular disease may be at greater risk.

? PENNSAID is contraindicated in the perioperative setting of coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery.

Gastrointestinal Risk

? NSAIDs cause an increased risk of serious gastrointestinal adverse events including bleeding, ulceration, and perforation of the stomach or intestines, which can be fatal. These events can occur at any time during use and without warning symptoms. Elderly patients are at greater risk for serious gastrointestinal events.

   PENNSAID is also contraindicated in patients:

?     With known hypersensitivity to diclofenac sodium or any other component of PENNSAID.

?     Who have experienced asthma, urticaria, or allergic-type reactions after taking aspirin or other NSAIDs. Severe, rarely fatal, anaphylactic-like reactions have been reported in these patients.

  Anaphylactoid reactions may occur in patients without prior exposure to PENNSAID. NSAIDs can cause serious skin adverse events such as exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson Syndrome (SJS), and toxic epidermal necrosis (TEN), which can be fatal.

The most common treatment-related adverse events in patients receiving PENNSAID were application site skin reactions including dry skin (32%), contact dermatitis characterized by skin erythema and induration (9%), contact dermatitis with vesicles (2%) and pruritus (4%). In a long term safety study, contact dermatitis occurred in 13% and contact dermatitis with vesicles in 10% of patients, generally within the first 6 months of exposure, leading to a withdrawal rate for an application site event of 14%. Other common adverse events greater than placebo include: dyspepsia (8%), abdominal pain (6%), flatulence (4%), diarrhea (4%) and nausea (4%).

FDA: Don't Tighten Vicodin Regulation
By David Pittman, Washington Correspondent; Kristina Fiore, Staff Writer, MedPage Today
Published: October 25, 2012

WASHINGTON -- Hydrocodone-containing combination products, such as hydrocodone/acetaminophen (Vicodin), should be kept as Schedule III controlled substances and not be subject to tighter regulations to prevent abuse, the FDA recommended Thursday.

There's insufficient evidence to support the Drug Enforcement Administration's (DEA) finding that hydrocodone-containing products have a similar abuse potential as Schedule II drugs and should be regulated as such, the FDA said in briefing documents released ahead of a public meeting next week on the issue.

"It is clear, however, from [FDA] analyses that combination hydrocodone-containing analgesics are widely abused, but no objective threshold exists to correlate levels of abuse with the level of scheduling," Silvia Calderon, PhD, team leader for pharmacology on the FDA's controlled substance staff, wrote in the documents.

Hydrocodone alone is already a Schedule II drug.

There have been a number of efforts to move hydrocodone combination products to Schedule II, which would put more stringent requirements on storage and prescribing, including limits on oral prescriptions and refills<http://www.medpagetoday.com/PublicHealthPolicy/PublicHealth/26098>.

The most recent effort on the federal level came as an amendment to the Senate's FDA user fee reauthorization bill. However, that provision was stripped<http://www.medpagetoday.com/Anesthesiology/PainManagement/33080> before the final bill was passed, and the two-day meeting being held in Silver Spring, Md., was the compromise for its deletion, according to Sen. Joe Manchin (D.-W.Va.).

And last June, New York state passed a law<http://www.medpagetoday.com/PublicHealthPolicy/PublicHealth/33216> that will make hydrocodone combination products schedule II drugs.

But the charge to up-schedule these drugs has spanned more than a decade<http://www.medpagetoday.com/Blogs/InOtherWords/29102>, with the DEA receiving a Citizen's Petition in 1999 to investigate the issue.

In 2004, the DEA asked the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to look into a schedule change, and HHS concluded in 2008 that hydrocodone combo products could remain Schedule III drugs.

The following year, DEA asked the FDA's Center for Drug Evaluation and Research to re-evaluate drug abuse-related data for hydrocodone combination products, and the center's final analysis will be presented at a meeting of the agency's Drug Safety and Risk Management Advisory Committee on Monday and Tuesday.

The panel is comprised of the committee's regular members as well as a handful of temporary members who will have the opportunity to vote on whether to up-schedule or not.

Those temporary panelists include Perry Fine, MD, of the University of Utah, a former board member of the American Pain Foundation (APF), which shuttered last spring after reports of its financial ties<http://www.propublica.org/article/two-leaders-in-pain-treatment-have-long-ties-to-drug-industry> to the pharmaceutical industry. A Senate Finance Committee investigation into the ties between opioid drugmakers and various physician and advocacy groups is ongoing.

Other temporary panel members also include Angie Gravois, a pain patient who formerly spoke on behalf of the APF, Michael Fry, the pharmacy manager for Rite Aid Corp., and a handful of other pain specialists and chronic pain advocacy groups.

Those panelists are balanced by representatives from the CDC and other clinicians, including Lewis Nelson, MD, of New York University, who have been pushing for increased awareness of the prescription painkiller abuse epidemic<http://www.medpagetoday.com/PublicHealthPolicy/HealthPolicy/32355>.

An FDA spokesperson said it's not unusual to include temporary voting members, though it's not routine for every drug safety advisory committee.

In its own risk analysis study, which it released online ahead of the meeting, the FDA found more emergency department visits and more toxic exposures with oxycodone combination products -- such as oxycodone/acetaminophen (Percocet) -- than hydrocodone combos.

It also highlighted similar initiation rates for both products, and concluded that it "could not find data to support DEA's assertion that the addition of acetaminophen to hydrocodone tablets does not deter abuse."

The FDA and DEA noted that it's difficult to ascertain the abuse of specific hydrocodone combination products, since there is no single national system for collecting data on both events representing abuse and a measurable population exposed to risk.

The FDA outlined a number of other reasons against up-scheduling hydrocodone.

There could be an increase in the use of nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) if these other drugs are up-scheduled and therefore become harder to prescribe.

Also, with their usual Schedule III drugs now on Schedule II, providers may be more likely to prescribe Schedule II opioids more frequently, the agency charged.

In addition, codeine-containing cough suppressants would be the sole option among antitussive opioid combination Schedule III products with the up-schedule.

Should the schedule change occur, clinicians will face greater barriers to prescribing the drug. Schedule II drugs must be handwritten and pharmacies must have the original prescription in hand before dispensing. Also in many states, mid-level practitioners are not authorized to prescribe Schedule II drugs.

But critics are still concerned that hydrocodone combination products are just as addictive as oxycodone combination products, which already fall under Schedule II.

"FDA doesn't need to go much further than [a handful of published journal] articles to conclude that Vicodin belongs in the same schedule as Percocet," Andrew Kolodny, MD, chair of psychiatry at Maimonides Medical Center in New York, told MedPage Today.

Still, FDA concluded that "alternatives to up-scheduling may also decrease the levels of abuse and misuse of these products." And an analysis from the Generic Pharmaceutical Association, included in the meeting preview documents, similarly concluded that "drug abuse is a complex problem that is not likely to be addressed by rescheduling of drugs or other regulations."

Several groups, including Advocates for the Reform of Prescription Opioids and Save the Michaels of the World, plan to protest against FDA's stance during the meeting.
