The Opioid Abuse Deterrence Act and DOJ Initiatives: Just What the Doctor Ordered?

Posted: 07 Dec 2017 08:48 PM PST

By John A. Gilbert & Larry K. Houck  

 For Americans under the age of 50, drug overdoses are now the leading cause of death.  DOJ, Attorney General Jeff Sessions Delivers Remarks Announcing New Tools to Combat the Opioid Crisis (Nov. 29, 2017) (here).   With evidence suggesting that nearly 80 percent of individuals addicted to heroin started out on opioid pain relievers, the link is clear that opioid prescriptions are driving this epidemic.   Rep. Mark Meadows, Opioid Abuse Deterrence, Research and Recovery Act (here).  These statements by government officials, one representing the Trump Administration, the other from Congress, provide a sobering picture of the nationwide opioid abuse epidemic and form the basis for two new actions designed to stem the opioid crisis.  On November 29, 2017, Congressman Mark Meadows (R-NC) introduced H.R. 4482, the Opioid Abuse Deterrence, Research, and Recovery Act of 2017.  On the same day, Attorney General Jeff Sessions announced several Department of Justice ( DOJ ) and Drug Enforcement Administration ( DEA ) efforts also aimed at addressing the crisis.

Opioid Abuse Deterrence, Research, and Recovery Act of 2017

The Opioid Abuse Deterrence, Research and Recovery Act ( the Act ) would amend the Federal Controlled Substances Act ( CSA ) to require DEA-registered and state-licensed practitioners authorized to prescribe schedule II or III controlled substances to submit a  certification  to DEA that they will not prescribe a schedule II or III opioid  for the initial treatment of acute pain  unless the prescribed quantity is for less than seven days or falls within a State-established prescription limit.  Acute pain  is defined as  pain with abrupt onset and caused by an injury or other process that is diagnostically determined to have minimal risk of escalating in intensity.    Acute pain  under the Act does not include chronic pain, pain treated as part of cancer care, hospice, end-of-life care, or palliative care.

Under the Act, the certification would not prevent practitioners from prescribing opioids approved by FDA for opioid use disorder treatment; for immediate, post-operative pain relief; or for longer than seven days if prescribing is consistent  with a clear medical standard of care,  provided that the practitioner documents the prescription in the patient s medical record and consults the State electronic health record system or prescription drug monitoring program.

The legislation would also require the FDA Commissioner to continue working with stakeholders and encouraging the development of abuse-deterrent opioids. In addition, to understand what led to the opioid crisis, the Act requires the Comptroller General to submit a report to Congress within two years on the health care policy changes that may have contributed to the increase in opioid overdoses and deaths.  The report must include:

A review of the federal health care-related legislative, administrative, and judicial decisions that affected access to pharmaceutical pain management strategies;
An analysis of the financial and non-financial costs and benefits of reversing or revising such decisions;
An analysis of the differences between State prescription drug monitoring programs;
 An analysis of the impacts of State and Federal prescribing limitations on patient medical outcomes; and
An analysis of the costs of using abuse-deterrent opioids compared to non-abuse-deterrent opioids.

Finally, the Act would require the FDA Commissioner to conduct a study on the feasibility of replacing the prescribing limits in the bill  with evidence-based clinical guidelines,  including a limitation  on the first opioid prescription for patients for an acute pain diagnosis  and  the incorporation into routine medical visits of evidence-based screening tools [to monitor] the misuse of opioids and other controlled substances. 

HPM Comments

We have long believed that effectively addressing the opioid epidemic requires focus on the physicians, doctors, dentists, and other practitioners who are the gatekeepers of public access to controlled substances. It is clear that overprescribing or inappropriate prescribing of controlled substances has been a significant cause in creating and sustaining the opioid abuse crisis.

The Act was clearly drafted with the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention s ( CDC s ) Guidelines for Prescribing Opioids for Chronic Pain in mind. While the CDC guidelines voluntarily limit opioid prescribing for chronic pain, the Act limits only the first or initial prescription of schedule II or III opioids to treat acute pain to seven days unless the practitioner fulfills requirements to prescribe for a longer period.  In fact, the Act does not reference prescribing for chronic pain.  Both the Act and the CDC guidelines focus on a theme that we believe is a significant contributor to the opioid abuse problem, that is, overprescribing or inappropriate prescribing of controlled substances.  However, the mechanics of having a prescriber provide a  certification  to DEA is problematic.  There are no details on how prescribers would  certify  (e.g., during the application or renewal process).  More importantly, the Act does not address the regulatory effect of certifying or, even more significantly, failure to comply with the certification.  It also fails to address whether practitioners will self-certify or obtain certification for submission from an official or unofficial organization.  It is worth noting that the CSA and DEA regulations related to sales of pseudoephedrine, provide for a certification by retail sellers that they will not sell in amounts greater than allowed under the CSA.  21 U.S.C.   830(e)(1)(A)(vii); 21 C.F.R.    1314.35-.42, 1314.101-.103.  Regardless, the Act s requirements will make practitioners more carefully consider issuing a first opioid prescription for longer than seven days.  The inescapable downside is that some overly cautious practitioners may decline to issue necessary prescriptions to legitimate patients for longer than a week if they do not want to adhere to the requirements to do so or from fear that they will appear on DEA s radar.

We believe that mandatory training and education for practitioners is more critical and an alternative would be to require that all practitioners who intend to be registered with DEA to prescribe Schedule II controlled substances should certify that they have received such training.

DOJ and DEA Initiatives

Attorney General Sessions announced several initiatives including a restructuring of DEA Field Offices to focus on the opioid abuse problem. The Attorney General announced that DOJ was awarding $12 million to law enforcement agencies in states hit hard by illegal prescription opioid, heroin, and methamphetamine activity.  DOJ awarded $7 million through its Anti-Heroin Task Force Program to investigate heroin and illegal opioid distribution in states with high per capita levels of treatment admissions for heroin and other opioids, and $5 million through the Anti-Methamphetamine Program to states that have  demonstrated numerous seizures of precursor chemicals, finished methamphetamine, laboratories, and laboratory dump seizures.  DOJ, Attorney General Sessions and Acting DEA Administrator Patterson Announce New Tools to Address Opioid Crisis (Nov. 29, 2017) (here).

Attorney General Sessions also announced the formation of a new DEA Louisville Field Division. This new office will strengthen DEA investigation and enforcement efforts under a single Special Agent in Charge in Kentucky, Tennessee, and West Virginia.  The geographic area served by the new Louisville Field Division was previously distributed among the Detroit, Atlanta, and Washington, D.C., Field Divisions.  The Attorney General anticipates that consolidating Kentucky, Tennessee, and West Virginia within a single jurisdiction  will produce more effective investigations on heroin, fentanyl, and prescription opioid trafficking, all of which have a significant impact on the region.  Id.

Lastly, the Attorney General directed every U.S. Attorney to designate an Opioid Coordinator for their district by December 15th. The Attorney General s memo to all U.S. Attorneys instructed that Opioid Coordinators will be responsible for:

Facilitating intake of cases involving prescription opioids, heroin, and fentanyl;
Convening a task force of federal, state, local, and tribal law agencies to identify opioid cases for federal prosecution, facilitate interdiction efforts, and tailor their district s response to the needs of their communities;
Advising and training Assistant United States Attorneys on prosecuting opioid offenses;
Maintaining statistics on opioid prosecutions; and
Developing and evaluating the strategy to combat the opioid epidemic.

HPM Comments  

The creation of a new DEA Field Office focuses on several states particularly hard hit by the opiate abuse problem. Thus, it makes sense that DEA would consolidate resources to narrow the geographic scope to address these issues.  DEA drug investigations are better coordinated and more efficient when conducted within a single Field Division rather than multiple jurisdictions.  It also seems to us that the creation of an Opioid Coordinator should result in a more focused approach by U.S. Attorney offices to the opioid problem.  We note that in August 2017 the Attorney General had announced the formation of the Opioid Fraud and Abuse Detection Unit, which is a pilot program funding 12 prosecutors nationwide to focus on investigating and prosecuting health care fraud related to prescription opioids. Thus, DOJ/DEA is devoting significant resources to the fight against opioid abuse, which will likely result in more criminal, civil and administrative actions.

Subject: OFIRMEV Advocacy Plan (for Review)



 

Mike & Mike,

 

Attached is the final draft OFIRMEV Advocacy plan, which incorporates Advocacy and Federal/State initiatives to address opioid-associated adverse events in the perioperative setting.

 

The adverse events associated with the overuse of opioids in the hospital is a threat to patient safety, our health care institutions and contributes to an increase in overall healthcare cost.  To address this national concern, the Advocacy/Government Affairs team will engage in a series of national and state initiatives that instill awareness and create a sense of urgency that in order to reduce the overuse of opioids, multimodal analgesia (MMA) needs to be the accepted and preferred standard of care in the perioperative setting.

 

We will accomplish this by focusing on four strategic areas:

1.       Address need to minimize hospital (institutional)/ provider risk (risk management; quality)

2.       Improve overall patient safety by minimizing adverse events, length of stay and readmissions

3.       Ensure needs of high risk patients in elderly populations are addressed

4.       Focus on individualized patient care (right product, right patient) to advance access to MMA

 

Please take some time to review the attached plan, and we would value your feedback and comments.  I will also set a call so that we can discuss the Advocacy plan in greater detail.

Subject:Peculiar Orders
I just had a meeting with the CDIG group and as we discussed our relationship, how their systems work
and what their systems manage, we may have stumbled across something that should be considered as
part of our Peculiar Orders process.
Apparently over the course of a company s life, different aspects of the information associated with their
DEA license registration will change, i.e., they move to a different location; they change their name; they
change owners. Conceivably there could be a company that s been around for 50 years doing business for
us but if they move, CDIG sets them up with a new customer number so they appear to be a new
customer. I would think it would benefit our regulatory stewardship to be able to maintain the genealogy
of a specific company over the lifetime of their business with us. This would aid a new CSR in knowing
that this is a customer with whom we ve had a long lasting relationship but could also be a red flag of a
company who s in trouble financially and is trying to fly under the radar by moving frequently or changing
their name a lot. We simply update a customer record and add an  effective date  for  each change to the
record to create the links through all of the identities under which a company has done business and/or
locations at which this company may have operated. To have the ability to do this, we d have to
incorporate a change to the CDIG files to add the  affectivity date  for maintain historical information on
the customers.

Best Regards,

On Apr 26, 2013, at 9:43 AM, "Nosco, Dennis L" <Dennis.Nosco@Covidien.com<mailto:Dennis.Nosco@Covidien.com>> wrote:

Colleagues,

I wanted to share with you a new initiative that Anthony Lassiter and I feel is crucial to moving forward as an independent pharmaceutical company.

That initiative is the creation of a Label Review Committee (LRC).  This committee would be responsible for three major areas:


1)     Driving changes to labels (i.e., package inserts) globally (and, in some cases, regionally) based on new information and/or requests from either internal (e.g., from our Signal Action Committee or other internal sources like the CCSI working group (see below)) or external (e.g., FDA or O-US regulatory agencies) sources.

2)     Approving company core safety information (sometimes referred to as CCDS or CCSI) documents.  These documents, common throughout the pharmaceutical industry but lacking for all but a couple (Optimark and Optiray) of our products, contain the core safety concepts that the company feels should appear in all labels, globally, for a product.   These documents are currently being generated by our relatively newly-formed CCSI working group.  The first one will be ready for approval by the second week in May at the latest.

3)     Helping to ensure alignment of labels (globally) to CCSI content.  This includes aiding, if requested, in addressing questions from local regulatory personnel and/or local regulatory agencies as variations are filed to account for changes due to CCSI content.

Anthony and I have talked through this and we believe that the membership of this committee should be:

Regulatory/Global Labeling: Dennis Nosco, chairperson
Pharmacovigilance: Anthony Lassiter
Legal: Joe Wuestner
Commercial: (business head of area, either Imaging or Specialty Pharma)
Scientific Affairs: Alfredo Bozzini

This committee could also include ad hoc members from other areas (e.g., Regulatory Strategy and CMC Regulatory, PK, Clinical Studies) as their special expertise is needed.

By this e-mail I am asking if all of you would either (a) agree to be on this committee or (b) designate someone from your area to be the representative on this committee.

Once I get agreement as to membership I will call our first meeting.  The timing of formation of this committee is crucial as we have our first new CCSI document that is about ready to be submitted to the LRC for review.  In addition, we have a company initiative regarding EXALGO labeling and inclusion of abuse deterrent safety language that will require this committee s input on language and help on getting these changes implemented globally)

As timing is short to get this committee operational please get back to me AND Anthony with any questions you have.  I would like to set up our first meeting for sometime in the next 3 weeks.

Thanks,

Dennis Nosco, PhD, RAC

More specifically:

 

King Pharmaceuticals branded prescription drugs include Embeda® (morphine sulfate and naltrexone hydrochloride) Extended Release (ER) Capsules and Avinza® (morphine sulfate extended release), both with similar indications to EXALGO for moderate to severe around-the-clock pain for opioid-tolerant patients.

KG: Pain relief – Pfizer buying KG for $14.25/share; DOWNGRADING to HOLD from BUY

William Tanner, BioPharma
212-632-1512, william.tanner@lazardcap.com


*       Pfizer buying King; downgrading KG shares to HOLD from BUY. Pfizer announced its intention to acquire King for $14.25 per share in cash, a 40% premium to yesterday’s closing price for KG shares. We are downgrading KG shares to HOLD, as the stock is likely to trade above our fair value estimate.
*       Pain franchise likely most attractive to Pfizer, but Animal Health business may have appeal too. We suspect that the primary interest in King for Pfizer lies with King’s emerging abuse-deterrent opioid platform. Re-filing of Remoxy is expected by YE10 and we believe the drug could be on the market in 2011. Remoxy (oxycodone) should complement Embeda (morphine), the potentially abuse-deterrent pain drug that was launched in 2009. Given the existence of a broad animal health business, we suspect that King’s Animal Health business (approx. $350M+ per annum in revenues) may have been attractive, too.
*       Purchase price not impressive, but other bidders may be unlikely. The $3.6B purchase price values King at a price/sales multiple of 2.5x based on our 2011 sales estimate and an EV/EBIDTA multiple of 8.1x on our 2011 EBITDA estimate. Our DCF for King yields a fair value of $13 per share, which put the offer of $14.25 per share at only a 10% premium. Of note, our DCF included $3-$4 per share for Remoxy with peak sales of $600M+ and a launch in 2011, and thus did not reflect the regulatory and commercial risk associated with the drug. Pfizer announced that it is expecting significant cost savings from the transaction on the order of at least $200M per year realized by the end of 2013. Based on the size of these synergies, the offer appears to be at the low end of expectations. Since the transaction has been approved by the boards of both companies, unless another bidder materializes, we believe that the transaction will go through close to this price level.

From: Schooler, JoAnna S
Sent: Friday, March 25, 2011 9:21 AM
To: Littlejohn, Stephen E
Subject: Update on Monitoring of the Three Prescription Drug Abuse Bills



 

Steve,

 

Below are the summaries of the three bills recently introduced – two in the Senate and one in the House of Representatives.  All three of these bills have been referred to committee.  Only the Pill Mill bill has been able to garner significant support thus far with a number of co-sponsors from Florida and Kentucky, where the issue has been most prevalent.  Currently, we don’t expect any of these three bills to move in the short-term with the ongoing budget debate occurring through April and May. In addition, the House Judiciary is starting on patent reform next week, so that will take up most of that committee’s time in the short term.  

 

We were already working with the D.C. office to set up meetings for Herb that will target people on Capitol Hill who have been most active in the prescription drug abuse debate for introductory and follow-up meetings on C.A.R.E.S. Alliance.  In light of these recent bills, we plan to refine our talking points to address positive initiatives in the proposal along with outlining our concerns.  The D.C. office has been enlisted to monitor these bills and we’re scheduling a session with several members of the PPS team, Legal, our D.C. office and others from the Commercial Team to discuss these in further detail early next week.  We will be able to provide another update on our plans with more specifics next week.  Please let me know if you have any questions or need additional information.

 

 

S. 507 – Prescription Drug Abuse Prevention and Treatment Act of 2011

 

Reintroduced by Senator Jay Rockefeller on March 8, this is an updated version of the Methadone Treatment and Prevention Act that was introduced in 2010. It calls for new training requirements for health care providers, consumer education campaigns, increased Federal support for state prescription drug monitoring programs and reporting of opioid-related deaths, as well as basic clinical guidelines for the safe use and dosage of pain medications.  The bill was referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions. It currently lacks co-sponsors. Below are some details on the specific proposals:

 

-    Provider Education - Require the Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) to establish a mandatory and comprehensive practitioner education program for methadone and other opioids, in collaboration with relevant professional societies.  Completion of this education program will be required as part of the Drug Enforcement Administration’s (DEA) current registration process used to authorize practitioners to prescribe, dispense and administer controlled substances. Currently, there is no federal education requirement for prescribers of these drugs.  Note: Internally, we believe this would be best addressed by adding training prescribing CII medications to medical school curriculum.

 

-    Consumer Education - Provide competitive grants to states and community organizations to educate consumers and communities about safe and appropriate use of prescription pain relievers, including methadone. Note: Internally, we believe that training on the risks of taking prescription medications for non-medical use should be added to school curriculum for grades 7-12.

 

-    Controlled Substances Clinical Standards Commission - Created the Controlled Substances Clinical Standards Commission to establish patient education guidelines, appropriate and safe dosing guidelines for all forms of methadone, benchmark guidelines for the reduction of methadone abuse, appropriate conversion factors for transition patients from one opioid to another, guidelines for the initiation of methadone for pain management, and consensus guidelines for the treatment of pain management with prescription opioids.  In creating such guidelines, the Clinical Standards Commission would be required to collaborate with outside experts, health care professional societies, patient representatives, and others.

 

-    National All Schedules Prescription Electronic Reporting Act (NASPER) -This legislation would appropriate $25 million a year for NASPER to establish interoperable prescription drug monitoring programs within each state. Currently, 38 states have enacted legislation requiring prescription drug monitoring programs (PMPs).

 

 

-    National Opioid Death Registry – Creates a National Opioid Death Registry to track all opioid-related deaths and related information.  Also, establish a standard form for medical examiners to fill out which would include information for the National Opioid Death Registry. Currently, there is no comprehensive national database of drug-related deaths in the United States, nor is there a standard form for medical examiners to fill out with regard to opioid-related deaths. Note: Internally, this is seen as extremely helpful for patient access by thwarting attempts to move to another scheduled drug to avoid educational requirements by prescribers.

 

-    ADDITIONAL Provisions

 

-    Opioid treatment programs – Will be required by law to make acceptable alternative arrangements for the safe distribution of methadone for patients who are not permitted take home doses on days where the clinic is closed. 

 

-    Moratorium on 40-mg Methadone Diskettes: For two years, no provider may prescribe and no pharmacy or opioid treatment clinic may distribute 40-mg methadone diskettes unless the prescription or dispensation is consistent with DEA policy.

 

-    Annual Report on Effectiveness: No later than September 30, 2012 the Secretary will report to Congress the effectiveness and evaluate the success of efforts to reduce opioid addiction and methadone-related deaths including the impact of health care provider and patient education.

 

 

H. 1065 – Pill Mill Crackdown Act of 2011

 

This legislation, introduced on March 14 by Representative Vern Buchanan (R-Fl) with bi-partisan co-sponsorship including the support of15 Florida members, amends the Controlled Substances Act to provide for increased penalties for operators of pill mills.  It calls for criminal forfeiture of the property of pill mill operators and use of property and the proceeds of any disposition of the property will be made available for use by the National Office of Drug Control Property.  Note: the current draft lacks a tight definition of a pill mill.

In addition, it amends the Controlled Substance Act to reschedule hydrocodone combination products from schedule III to the more restrictive schedule II designation, which are not refillable and require DEA Official Order Forms and increased security measures for dispensers. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, the Judiciary Committee, and the Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime, Terrorism, and Homeland Security

 

 

S. 513 – Saving Kids from Dangerous Drugs Act of 2011

 

This legislation, introduced on March 8, is aimed at fighting drug misuse and abuse by minors.  It amends the Controlled Substances Act to provide enhanced penalties for marketing controlled substances to minors. The bill was introduced by Senators Diane Feinstein (D-CA) and Chuck Grassley (R-IA).  It makes it illegal for any person more than 18 years old to combine a controlled substance with a beverage or candy product, to market or package a controlled substance to appear similar to a beverage or candy product or to modify a controlled substance with flavoring or coloring to distribute or sell to minors.  The only exceptions to the penalties is any controlled substance that is FDA approved if its contents, packaging and marketing has not been altered from the approved form or if it has been altered by a practitioner for a legitimate medical purpose in the usual course of professional practice. The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee.

DEA Announces “Groundbreaking” Guidance that is Inconsistent with the Settlement they are Announcing – Time at Last for Rulemaking?

 

By John A. Gilbert, Jr. –

On July 11, 2017, the Department of Justice and the Drug Enforcement Administration (“DEA”) announced that Mallinckrodt LLC, a pharmaceutical manufacturer, agreed to pay $35 million to settle allegations related to the adequacy of its efforts to detect and inform DEA of suspicious orders of controlled substances.  Although DEA has reached similar settlements with distributors and pharmacy chains (see, e.g., here), this is the first settlement of its kind with an opioid manufacturer.  DOJ’s press release states that the settlement reflects manufacturers’ obligation to monitor orders not only from their own customers, but also between distributors and pharmacies and clinics downstream in the distribution chain.  However, this statement appears  inconsistent with the language in the settlement document, marks a stark shift in the prevailing understanding of manufacturers’ suspicious order monitoring obligations and raises serious questions about the legal basis and workability of such a requirement.

For years, DEA has been criticized for failure to provide guidance on the suspicious order monitoring regulation, 21 C.F.R. § 1301.74(b).  The language in that section has remained unchanged since its enactment in 1971 and while DEA issued informal guidance letters to certain industry groups in 2006, 2007 and 2012,  DEA’s interpretation of that regulation has evolved significantly beyond that guidance.  More important, a fundamental deficiency in the regulation is that it fails to recognize the differences between manufacturers and distributors, including the level of data available to each concerning sales between distributors and pharmacies.  Thus, the lack of a clear regulation has continued to hinder industry’s ability to meet DEA’s expectations.

Unfortunately for industry, in the last several years, DEA has set forth its evolving view of the regulation primarily in presentations at conferences, through Memoranda of Agreement (“MOAs”) related to enforcement actions and in the Southwood and, more recently, the Masters decisions. (see, e.g., here and here).  While this approach has allowed DEA to avoid the notice and comment rulemaking requirement under the Administrative Procedure Act (“APA”), it has also left industry with little clarity about their obligations around the reporting of suspicious orders. A critical element of notice and comment rulemaking is for an agency to solicit important industry input on the impact of potential rulemaking, with the ultimate goal being effective and clear regulations.  Such clarity would result in a more secure supply chain for controlled substances, which would better serve the public interest as the U.S. continues to struggle with the issue of opioid diversion and abuse.

The press release concerning the Mallinckrodt settlement, which purported to set out “groundbreaking” new rules, is another example of DEA establishing a new standard while avoiding notice and comment rulemaking. 

The problem revolves around DEA’s discussion of chargebacks (which are a common pharmaceutical pricing feature), for the first time, and a critical discrepancy between the language set forth in the government’s press release and the obligation outlined in the MOA with Mallinckrodt.  (In general, a chargeback is a payment made by a manufacturer to a distributor to make the distributor whole when it sells the manufacturer’s product at a price below a specified rate. After a distributor sells a manufacturer’s product to the pharmacy, for example, it requests a chargeback from the manufacturer and to support that request for payment, the distributor identifies the product, volume and the pharmacy to which it sold the product.) In its press release, the government stated that, “[t]he groundbreaking nature of the settlement involves requiring a manufacturer to utilize chargeback and similar data to monitor and report to DEA suspicious sales of its oxycodone at the next level in the supply chain, typically sales from distributors to independent and small chain pharmacy and pain clinic customers.” (emphasis added). This appears to set forth DEA’s position that manufacturers must review chargebacks and report the underlying sales from the distributor to downstream pharmacies as suspicious orders.

However, we have reviewed Mallinckrodt’s MOA and it does not require reporting downstream transactions as suspicious orders.  Rather, the MOA provides that Mallinckrodt review chargeback data and alert DEA of pharmacies (not orders) that may be concerning.   The clear focus of the language is a reporting of pharmacies as a condition of the MOA, not the reporting of chargebacks as suspicious orders under 21 CFR 1301.74(b). Note, as of this writing, the MOA has not been posted to the government’s websites.

As an initial matter, it is not clear that DEA can create such a new requirement by announcing it in a press release. First, nothing in the language of 21 C.F.R. § 1301.74(b) suggests that a manufacturer must review orders between two downstream third parties and report them as suspicious. Second, we could find no prior public statement from DEA that a manufacturer must report such third party transactions as suspicious under 21 C.F.R. § 1301.74(b). Finally, if this really is “groundbreaking” – to use the government’s own word – surely such a change should warrant notice and comment rulemaking.

Moreover, there is no indication manufacturers’ attempts to monitor downstream transactions would be productive. It appears instead that manufacturers will be expected to second guess distributors’ decisions to fill orders from pharmacies (well after those sales have been completed), even though the manufacturers have far less information than the distributors have about those pharmacies. Distributors often have longstanding relationships with their pharmacy customers and sophisticated monitoring programs to evaluate pharmacy orders.  In contrast, a manufacturer can only see – after the fact – the manufacturer’s products a distributor sells to a pharmacy and for which the distributor submits a chargeback request. With such limited visibility, a simple and perfectly legitimate switch by a pharmacy from one manufacturer’s product to another’s, for example, could look like a suspicious “increase” in the distributor’s sales to that pharmacy. 

DEA’s position raises many additional practical questions. If the manufacturer and distributor disagree about which orders are suspicious, will DEA hold manufacturers’ reports of suspicious orders against the distributor, even if the distributor is better positioned to assess those orders?  How many orders that appear “suspicious” to a manufacturer can be filled by a distributor before the manufacturer must stop selling to that distributor?  And how should a manufacturer structure a program designed to monitor distributor sales to tens of thousands of pharmacies with which the manufacturer has no contact?

Manufacturers will likely be struggling with these issues for years to come. That ongoing confusion and its negative impact on the security of the supply chain emphasizes, once again, the need for DEA to make clear the obligations of manufacturers through notice and comment rulemaking on this critical issue, especially as the country continues to struggle with the problem of opioid diversion and abuse.

[RxNews] 7 Arizona Doctors lose Medicaid Contracts

7 Arizona doctors lose Medicaid contracts
AHCCCS dismissals come amid prescription probe
13 comments by Ken Alltucker - Apr. 10, 2012 06:37 PM
The Republic I azcentral.com
The state's Medicaid program said it has terminated the contracts of seven doctors who were top prescribers of powerful
pain pills and mental-health prescription drugs.
Their dismissals were made public as the result of an ongoing probe by U.S. Sen. Charles Grassley, R-lowa, of drugprescribing patterns in Medicaid programs across the country. Medicaid programs, which provide health care to the
nation's poor, reimburse doctors and practitioners. Grassley's probe centers on health-care professionals who prescribe
large amounts of pain pills and psychiatric drugs.
Of the seven doctors terminated from the Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System, Arizona's Medicaid program,
two faced criminal charges in connection with their prescribing patterns, three relinquished their medical licenses and two
no longer treat Medicaid patients, prompting AHCCCS to terminate their contracts due to inactivity over a 24-month
period.
In an April 3 letter to Grassley, AHCCCS Director Thomas Betlach highlighted his agency's efforts to participate in a multiagency investigation of Dr. Angelo Chirban, the Arizona Medicaid program's most prolific prescriber of the pain pills
oxycodone and OxyContin over fiscal 2008 and 2009.
Chirban and his ex-wife were charged in U.S. District Court in December with 130 counts in connection with writing
thousands of prescriptions for oxycodone and other pain medications for non-medical reasons.
Grassley earlier questioned AHCCCS' efforts to ferret out fraud, waste and abuse as the agency spends $650 million
each year on prescription drugs for Medicaid recipients. In a January letter to Betlach, Grassley said he had "concerns
about the oversight and enforcement of Medicaid abuse in your state."
Two years ago, Grassley requested that Arizona's Medicaid program provide data on the top prescribers of common
painkillers oxycodone, OxyContin and Roxicodone, as well as six anti-anxiety and mental-health drugs for fiscal 2008 and
2009.
The Iowa Republican made similar inquiries to all state Medicaid programs to bring attention to the potential of fraud and
abuse in prescribing patterns.
Grassley has since requested -- and received from Arizona -- the top prescribers of those drugs for fiscal 2010 and 2011.
He also asked Betlach one dozen questions about AHCCCS' efforts to curb excessive prescription writing.
Betlach said that the top prescribers of the mental-health drugs represented less than 2 percent of AHCCCS' total
prescription costs for 2010 and 2011.
He noted the mental-health drugs are prescribed for the 122,000 Arizonans enrolled in the state's behavioral healthservices program, and of those, 20 percent are adults diagnosed with serious mental illness and 32.5 percent are children
or adolescents.

MNKOI 0004232018

 Only one of the seven doctors whose license was terminated was a psychiatrist. Jennifer Suzanne Gunther, a Tucson
psychiatrist, said she no longer treats Medicaid patients in her new position with the Veterans Administration. AHCCCS
terminated Tucson pain-management physician Susan B. Fleming's license because she no longer treats Medicaid
patients.
Lloyd David Armold, a Tucson osteopathic physician, surrendered his license in 2010 after the Arizona Board of
Osteopathic Examiners restricted his ability to prescribe hydrocodone and morphine. Armold said the "board was bugging
me for doing alternative medicine," so he decided to retire.
Erol LeBlanc, a family practice doctor, had his license revoked by the Arizona Board of Osteopathic Examiners in
September, the board's records show. Tucson physician Margarita Martinez, who could not be reached, relinquished her
license in 2009.
AHCCCS also terminated its contract with Albert Yeh, a Golden Valley physician who pleaded guilty in January 2011 to
three felonies and was sentenced to 21/2 years in prison and five years' probation. He surrendered $2 million in cash and
agreed to pay more than $683,000 in restitution to AHCCCS.

From: Connel, Greg <greg.connel@fleishman.com>

Sent: Fri Jul 23 09:20:29 2010
Subject: FW: Project Lazerus
Hi Art:

 

Per the discussion at the break, below is a top line summary of Project Lazarus. We interviewed one of its founders as part of an awareness effort we’re developing Ohio Department of Health.

 

Please let us know if you’d like us to help with a deeper dive on this initiative or how it can be integrated into the CARES Alliance.

 

Thanks,

 

Greg

 

Project Lazarus in Wilkes County, N.C., is another example of a program designed with heavy emphasis on the community. According to Fred Wells Brason, the first objective of Project Lazarus was to raise awareness of the prescription drug abuse problem in the community so that residents understand the extent of the problem and the various contributing factors. To achieve this objective, his team identified the stakeholders within the community – schools, medical centers, civic organizations, the business community/Chamber of Commerce, law enforcement, etc. – and brought them to the table with the goal being that each of those stakeholders would then build awareness within their sphere of influence. Fred noted that the awareness-building process was underway for more than two years and that providing resources for the various stakeholders was critical to enable them to implement the work within the community.

 

Physician education and training was a central component of Project Lazarus in Wilkes County, N.C. Experts met with county physicians to provide training on pain and addiction, management of chronic pain patients, proper prescribing methods, identifying diversion and forged materials and protecting prescriptions. Project administrators also worked closely with hospitals in the county to encourage them to change their policies on narcotics dispensing. Because of the low population and rural setting of the county, pharmacies weren’t open past 11 p.m. as recently as two years ago. As a result, people with addiction issues would show up at the ER late at night to get prescription pain medications. In part because of the efforts of Project Lazarus, most hospitals in the county changed their policies and now refer patients to a primary-care doctor or a specialist if they have chronic pain. If they do dispense drugs, they give a small number of pills, typically enough for only two days. Because of these changes, people who are abusing now understand that the hospitals are not a source of prescription opiates.

 

Fred Wells Brason acknowledged that it took some convincing to get the hospitals on board with the new policies, mainly due to the oversight agencies’ evaluations based on measureable excellence scales. Although the potential exists for disgruntled patients to complain about not receiving the medications they felt they needed, the hospitals understand that prescription drug abuse is a community problem and view the policy shifts as a way that they can contribute to the solution.

 

While complete data on the impact of Project Lazarus should be available later this year, it’s worth noting that Wilkes County dropped from being the heaviest dispenser of prescription opiates in 2007 to eighth in the state in 2009. Fred views this as an indicator that the efforts to educate physicians and hospitals have resulted in more appropriate prescribing practices and more careful scrutiny of individuals trying to access prescription drugs for illicit use.

 

 

Fred was adamant that the type of campaign being implemented in Ohio needs to be built up from the community level. He feels that the paradigm and mindset of the entire community needs to shift in order for true changes to be made. In fact, he attributes much of Project Lazarus’ success to its focus on working the problem at the community level, looking at the dynamics of the community and dissecting them to see how they could make a difference. He described the approach as very logical rather than scientific and said that interestingly, state and Medicaid officials are now reaching out to the project organizers for guidance on how to replicate the model throughout the state.

Subject: GOP Spending Talks Meet Resistance; Tax Talks May Focus on AMT
From: BGOV Congress Tracker <alerts@bgov.com>
Date: Tue, 05 Dec 2017 20:20:54 +0000
To: derek.naten@mallinckrodt.com


{Bloomberg Government}  

 

 

GOP Spending Talks Meet Resistance; Tax Talks May Focus on AMT

By Zachary Sherwood | December 5, 2017 03:17PM ET | Bloomberg Government


House Republicans leaders face resistance to their stopgap funding plan, tax talks may focus on the alternative minimum tax, the nominee for next Federal Reserve chairman advances out of committee.

Here’s what Bloomberg Government is tracking in Congress so far today.

Year-End Spending Talks

Republican leaders’ plan to avoid a federal shutdown by funding the government past Friday has been thrown into disarray as House conservatives push back over the timing of a stopgap spending measure. 

The rift within the Republican ranks forced the Rules Committee to postpone its meeting scheduled for today on setting parameters of debate for the continuing resolution. Rules now plans to meet tomorrow.

House Republican leaders told their rank and file this morning they intend to pass a two-week CR through Dec. 22, Reps. Lamar Smith (R-Texas) and Mike Bost (R-Ill.) told reporters. The current stopgap bill runs through Friday. Members of the conservative House Freedom Caucus want the temporary patch to extend through Dec. 30.

House Speaker Paul Ryan (Wis.) wouldn’t say whether the continuing resolution would go until Dec. 22 or Dec. 30. "You’ll see when we bring the vote to the floor," he said at a press conference this morning. Read more from Jack Fitzpatrick in today’s budget and appropriations update.

Chief Senate Tax Writers Prefer AMT Repeal

Two influential GOP senators -- Rob Portman (Ohio), one of the chamber’s main tax writers, along with Orrin Hatch (Utah), chairman of the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee -- said their preference is to repeal the corporate AMT.

“I’m not a big AMT fan,” said Portman, who also wants to repeal the individual AMT. “I’d like to end up there, but we’ve got to do the back and forth with the House.” Hatch added: “I’d like to get rid of it.”

In a last-minute change, the Senate bill preserved the corporate AMT at its current 20 percent rate, along with a modified version of the individual AMT. The House legislation repeals both levies.

Sen. David Perdue (R-Ga.), said he too would like to see the AMT eliminated for corporations and individuals by the House-Senate conference committee that’s expected to begin working out compromise legislation this week. “We couldn’t go all the way because we needed the revenue,” Perdue said, referring to the corporate AMT. Repealing it would have cost about $40 billion over a decade -- which shows just how close tax writers were to hitting the $1.5 trillion deficit limit set by their budget resolution.

House Ways and Means Chairman Kevin Brady (R-Texas), who’s overseeing the conference committee, said repealing the corporate AMT is “one of the priorities” for the conference.

Also, the repeal of the individual mandate requirement that’s part of the 2010 Affordable Care Act -- a feature of the Senate bill, but not the House legislation -- is still under discussion, but is likely to have strong support among House Republicans, Brady said.

Other negotiations will center on the temporary nature of the individual tax cuts in the Senate plan, with Brady acknowledging “we can’t achieve permanency in everything.” Catch up on all of today’s tax talk here.

PUBLIC OPINION: Opinion polls suggest a majority of voters aren’t happy with what they’ve seen. Fifty-three percent of U.S. voters disapprove of the Republican overhaul plan, and 64 percent say it favors the wealthy, according to a Quinnipiac University poll released today. The poll was conducted from Nov. 29 to Dec. 4.

DEMOCRATS’ OPPOSITION: The tax overhaul bill is likely to pass, but Congress will revisit parts of it in January and February, Rep. Richard Neal (D-Mass.), the House Ways and Means Committee’s top Democrat, said. “This is more about a need for a political victory than it is for tax reform,” he said at a breakfast meeting of the New England Council, a regional group of business leaders. “We will revisit a lot of these items next year. You accountants and attorneys, you are going to be busy.”

Neal, the ranking Democrat on the conference committee, said he goes into the process with an open mind. Members who go into conference announcing that they are opposed to the bill are marginalized, he said. That said, he doesn’t expect any Democrats to vote in favor of the bill. “It’s a tax cut, let’s call it what it is. I think when people find out who’s going to pay for these cuts, I’m not sure they will be so enthusiastic,” he said. Read more from Aaron Nicodemus.

More Legislation to Watch

IMMIGRATION: A group of House Republicans are seeking legislation that would allow undocumented immigrants brought to the U.S. as children to stay under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program. “Reaching across the aisle to protect DACA recipients before the holidays is the right thing to do,” Reps. Scott Taylor (R-Va.), Dan Newhouse (R-Wash.), Mia Love (R-Utah) and Mark Amodei (R-Nev.) said in a letter to Ryan signed by 30 other House Republicans.

Meanwhile, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) was encouraged by bipartisan talks on immigration and border security. "We think we’re moving in the right direction there," Schumer told reporters of efforts to bolster border security, and find a way to shield "dreamers" from deportation.

BIODIESEL CREDIT: Sen. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) said he has a promise from fellow senators to reinstate a lapsed $1-per-gallon biodiesel tax credit that expired at the end of 2016. That doesn’t include a promise to convert it into a producers credit, Grassley said in a conference call with reporters. Critics say the change is needed as historic structure of biodiesel tax incentive as blender’s credit subsidizes foreign production. Read more from Jennifer A. Dlouhy.

SECRET SERVICE OT: Secret Service agents would be eligible for additional overtime this year and next under legislation the House passed today. The Secret Service Recruitment and Retention Act (H.R. 3731) would raise the current cap on agents’ salaries, including overtime, from about $162,000 to $187,000 this year. The cap would rise again in calendar 2018 based on the salary in effect for federal employees at Level 2 of the Executive Schedule. Read more from Louis C. LaBrecque.

D.C. METRO BILL: A bill to overhaul the board of Washington’s public transit agency offers a 50 percent increase in federal funding but only if there are substantial reductions in spending on the union workforce. The bill (H.R. 4534) would take the Washington Area Metropolitan Transit Authority from a 16-member board to a five-member board. It was introduced yesterday by Rep. Barbara Comstock (R-Va.), whose constituents live in the Washington suburbs served by the Metro subway and bus lines. Read more from Mara Lee. 

Nominations Watch

FED CHAIRMAN: Federal Reserve Governor Jerome Powell, facing a Senate committee vote on his nomination to become the central bank’s chairman, won strong bipartisan support that suggests he’ll sail through the full Senate. The Senate Banking Committee voted 22-1 today in favor of Powell’s nomination. The lone no vote was from Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), who voiced concern before the tally was taken that he’d weaken financial regulations. Read more from Randall Woods.

DHS CHIEF: The Senate plans to vote at 4 p.m. on President Donald Trump’s nomination of Kirstjen Nielsen to serve as head of the Department of Homeland Security, Cornyn’s office said in a statement. If confirmed, Nielsen would fill the slot left vacant when John Kelly became White House chief of staff.

ENERGY RESEARCH: Linda Capuano, the nominee to be administrator of the Energy Information Administration, told lawmakers today she isn’t taking a position on climate change: “For me to take a position would introduce a bias.” Capuano faced questions on her position on climate change from Democrats during her Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee confirmation hearing. Capuano is Trump’s pick to be head of the independent statistical research arm of the Energy Department.

“The EIA provides unbiased data to inform those kinds of discussions. They’re very complex and the environment is very important,” Capuano said. “As the administrator of EIA, if I am appointed, it would not be wise for me to take a position on any particular issue, but to make sure that accurate and credible data is provided so that those issues can be debated and discussed.” Read more from Rebecca Kern.

What Else to Know Today

OPIOID FUNDING: Federal agencies need funding through appropriations to address aspects of the opioid crisis such as research of alternative medication and oversight of insurance company compliance, witnesses said at a hearing on preventing, treating, and recovering from opioid abuse. Democratic senators and witnesses from federal agencies also urged President Trump to take decisive actions to identify resources to reduce opioid misuse and to declare the crisis a national emergency rather than a public health emergency. They spoke at a Senate Appropriations Labor, Health and Human Services, Education and Related Agencies subcommittee hearing. Read more from Sara Merken.

CONYERS RESIGNS: Rep. John Conyers (D-Mich.), the longest serving House member, announced today that he’s leaving Congress immediately amid allegations that he sexually harassed members of his staff. "I am retiring today," said Conyers, who was also the top Democrat on the House Judiciary Committee. Conyers made the announcement in an interview with a Detroit radio station. Last week, House Minority Leader Nancy Pelosi (D-Calif.) and other Democratic leaders called for his resignation because of the accusations he abused staff members.

He said he’s endorsing his son, John Conyers III, to replace him in the safe Democratic seat, where a special election will be held. "I want you to know my legacy will continue through my children," he said. But there could be a family feud developing. Ian Conyers, a Michigan state senator and the congressman’s grand-nephew, told the New York Times that he plans to run for the Detroit-area seat. Read more from Billy House and Jackie Edwards.

MOORE PROBE: Senate Majority Leader Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) said today that Alabama’s Republican Senate Candidate, Roy Moore, could face a Senate Ethics Committee probe if he wins next week’s special election. "If he were to be elected I think he would immediately have an issue with the ethics committee which they would take up," McConnell told reporters. "We’ll see what happens after that," McConnell said.

EXALGO  Promotion Update

 

Hi Team:

 

At the One Mallinckrodt National Sales Meeting, we discussed the assumptions around the launch of a generic version of EXALGO.  We had previously communicated that due to a settlement agreement, Actavis could come to market with generic versions of the 8, 12 and 16 mg tablets as early as

November 15th, 2013.  At this time, Actavis has NOT received FDA approval and we do not believe they be launching soon.

 

What does this mean for me?

{*}       Keep the momemtum in your current territory.  We must focus on the products in our bag today.

I attach the updated Long-Term Evaluation Webinar Slides. 

 

For those of you who haven’t been present on recent Tri-Team calls but plan to attend, a big welcome and a note on the dynamic behind this Assessment.  

 

For the Metrics team, it may help to contrast this with the prescriber survey, where we found smart people, told them what FDA required of us and provided additional guidance, and paid them to do it.  We need to tread more delicately with the CE community, especially since providers are not all contractually obligated to field the survey with their completers. 

 

For the CE team, it may be helpful to note that FDA just provided 20 detailed comments to the patient survey protocol with expectations that we revise appropriately and may do the same with the LTE survey instrument.  The fact that the CE community typically operates at a distance from industry does not automatically relax “Metrics-oriented” FDA expectations/requirements.

 

In general, we are aiming to strike an appropriate balance and to convince the CE stakeholders that our preferred collaboration model is agreeable.  They may offer helpful input and it may be important to be flexible in some places (no FDA requirement) and firm in others (FDA requirement).

Subject: RE: Geisinger....
From: "Webb, Kevin J" <kevin.webb@mallinckrodt.com>
Date: Tue, 19 Jan 2016 22:59:23 +0000
To: "Price, Derek" <derek.price@mallinckrodt.com>


Hi Derek,

 

Good hearing from you again and hope you re having a good start to the new year. 

 

Following are key points from my recent phone calls with Craig Campbell, Director, Competitive Grants at Geisinger Health System Foundation.  Included on the calls were Eric Write (didn t catch his title):

 

          Initial exploratory call with Craig and Eric occurred ~Nov 17.  This was high level discussion in which we discussed Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals efforts to address opioid safe use, storage and disposal.  It was also opportunity to understand more about Geisinger s planned prescription drug disposal pilot program with their hospital system pharmacies

          Follow up call December 2 with Craig Campbell seeking funding to sponsor their research.  While we couldn t make funding available, we offered to provide them several thousand of the medication inactivation pouches

          Over the next few weeks had conversations with the following groups, and then made favorable introductions to Craig to assist them in the ensuring a successful pilot program

o   December 7; Community Anti-Drug Coalitions of America (CADCA).  CADCA is piloting a drug disposal pilot program in Florida to determine what triggers a desired behavior change in patients to willingly dispose of unused opioid medications.  Measuring three behavior influencers to dispose of unused opioids: patient/family safety; community safety/minimize diversion/prevent harm to the environment.  Ideally CADCA could share with Craig some of their measure processes

o   December 17; Delaware Pilot Disposal Program.  Due to our relationship with Verde Manufacturer (produce the inactivation pouch), Verde agreed to share with Geisinger the protocols of the drug disposal pilot program that Verde entered into with Delaware Department of Public Health.  It involved ~7 pharmacies but it had measurement tools in place to implement a successful program

o   December 18; Cardinal Health.  Made favorable introduction between Craig Campbell and Betsy Walker, Director of Community Relations at Cardinal Health.  Cardinal has a program called Generation Rx, and they make funding available to non-profit organizations to support education and awareness of community drug disposal programs.  This should be able to provide Geisinger the funding they need to launch a successful pilot program.

 

The last contact I had with Craig and Geisinger was December 18. 

 

I need to follow up with them and see if they re still interested in receiving the medication disposal pouches.  But I believe with the contacts we provided we can help get them to a successful disposal pilot should they decide to implement such a program. 

 

I m sorry you didn t know about this last month.  I had provided this in an update to Mike before the Christmas break but perhaps emails crossed and it didn t make it to you.

 

Let me know if you have any questions.


Thanks.

Kevin

Subject: EXALGO UPDATE



Gentlemen

Neuromed received initial comments on the Prescribing Information and the Medication Guide. We have not received correspondence or any REMS material.
I have read through the PI and Medication Guide and am writing to provide a brief update.

I am keeping the distribution of the message to a minimum because I think Neuromed should be the one to formally communicate this to Covidien.

There are many comments in the PI and some in the Medication Guide. Nearly all of the comments are consistent with our original submission but represent slight modifications of the labeling to be more consistent with embeda.  This is great news, as it means the recommended changes should be easy to accept and implement.  

In the Medication Guide the majority of changes are 1) changing  doctor  to  healthcare provider , 2) moving language from one section to another [the information in the Most important increases] 3) taking out Exalgo Alliance language, or 4) modifying our proposed language slightly to be consistent with embeda. I should note that the differences between formulation between embeda and EXALGO appear to play out in the  Important  box in the Medication Guide. Embeda only has one of the 4 bullets we have (one is for opioid tolerance and the other two are for protect from theft and swallow whole.

For the PI the types of changes are similar with some notable highlights:
The boxed warning has minimal recommended changes to language (and highlights the importance of  Proper Patient Selection )
The Indication (remove  intended for once-daily administration )
The indication is substantially smaller than our proposed indication and highlights opioid tolerance and not intended for prn analgesia. This removes contraindication for acute and post-operative pain and the should not be used to treat mild or short term pain (although this is elsewhere)
The agency requested to change the dosage range from 12-64mg to 8-64mg
The 5:1 potency ratio is kept
As expected, the 50-75% starting dose adjustment is being recommended to change to 50%
The have recommended a caution for medication errors between the 8 mg IR and 8mg EXALGO dosages
There is a request to modify the conversion table which cuts down on repetition in the PI
They have requested to modify a figure and a table. Both are easily modified but Figure 4 will not look as good (and it did not look great to begin with)
They kept the language on gradual onset of initial dose and have even asked for a bit more



This list is not comprehensive but is meant to give you highlights on what the agency has requested. Assuming there are no other outstanding requests and that Neuromed and Covidien can come to agreement (and get approval from J&J) quickly, I see no reason why these requests should hold up an on time approval.

We still need to hear about the REMS information but our assumption is still that we are getting the embeda REMS.

Best regards,
Rod

As discussed yesterday, we’re doing benchmarking now through our external advisors on our spend vs. other similarly situation companies, and very early signs, subject to change, are that we’re at the lower end.  Copying Matt/Cole/Nancy in the event we get inquiries on our reportable spend on federal lobbying.

Ackman Was Right: Valeant Skimps on Washington Lobbyists (1)

·         Underinvesting in government relations a `meaningful mistake'

·         Drugmaker spent $60,000 on lobbying in third quarter of 2015

By Anna Edney | November 5, 2015 10:04AM ET

(Updates with trading in eighth paragraph.)

Bill Ackman was right: Valeant Pharmaceuticals International Inc. spends a fraction of what similar drugmakers do on lobbyists to represent the company in Washington and keep it abreast of sentiment on the industry in the nation’s capital.

Valeant, under fire for price hikes on older drugs and a now-terminated relationship with a mail-order pharmacy that helped boost insurer reimbursement, faces investigations in both houses of the U.S. Congress. Yet the drugmaker, valued at $32 billion, is using very little of its $8.26 billion in 2014 sales on government relations, according to data compiled by Bloomberg Government.

Ackman, whose Pershing Square Capital Management is a top Valeant shareholder, said last week that Valeant had underinvested in government relations, a “meaningful mistake.”

Shire Plc and Endo International Plc, the two specialty pharmaceutical companies closest to Valeant in market value, spent $320,000 and $260,000 during the third quarter on lobbying. Valeant spent $60,000 in the same period and didn’t even have its own internal lobbyist.

‘Vulnerable to Attack’

“Shareholders need to understand the business and the progress of the company and really need to hear about bad news pronto,” Ackman, whose Pershing Square Capital Management owns 5.7 percent stake in Valeant, said Oct. 30 on a call about the company. “Anything less than complete transparency makes the company vulnerable to attack, and Valeant’s had its share of critics over the years.”

Valeant’s $60,000 went to the firm Mehlman Castagnetti Rosen & Thomas, which lobbied on tax, investment and labor issues. On Sept. 30, Valeant terminated Jeffrey J. Kimbell & Associates, which lobbied on pharmaceutical issues, according to Bloomberg Government.

Those two lobbyist firms, along with Valeant, Endo and Shire, didn’t respond to requests for comment. An outside spokesman for Ackman said he had no further comment.

Valeant shares fell 8.1 percent to $84.51 at 9:58 a.m. in New York, the lowest intraday price since June 2013.

Mehlman Castagnetti’s disclosure form says it lobbies for Valeant on “corporate structure, treatment of international income, reforms targeting internationally acquired companies.” Valeant has its tax domicile in Laval, Quebec, and its principal executive offices in New Jersey.

Kimbell was used for “pharmaceuticals and general FDA issues,” the firm said in its filing, without specifying further.

Lobbyists aren’t required to register that they started work for a company for 45 days, so it’s unclear whether Valeant has hired any other firms to advocate for them on drug pricing.

Hill Intelligence

In addition to bending the ear of lawmakers, lobbyists “can also provide intelligence from the Hill so that, before a company adopts a policy, they can have the benefit of ‘This is how it’s going to look to X, Y, Z, who matter,”’ said Len Nichols, director of the Center for Health Policy Research and Ethics at George Mason University.

Valeant has spent $200,000 total on lobbying in the first three quarters of this year, compared with $970,000 for Shire and $1.1 million for Endo. Pfizer Inc., with a market value of $216 billion, spent $6.5 million on lobbying in the first three quarters, according to Bloomberg Government data.

Turing Pharmaceuticals AG, also taking heat for raising the price of an older drug, hired Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney on Sept. 29 to lobby on pharmacy issues.

Seeking Subpoenas

In the U.S. House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, Democrats are pushing for a vote on Nov. 17 to subpoena the chief executive officers of Valeant and Turing to hand over documents on price increases. The lawmakers also want Committee Chairman Jason Chaffetz to hold a hearing on the issue.

Valeant raised the prices of two heart drugs, Nitropress and Isuprel,by 212 percent and 525 percent the day the drugmaker acquired the rights to sell them. Closely held Turing bought a decades-old anti-parasitic treatment and increased the price to $750 a pill from $13.50.

In the Senate, the Special Committee on Aging sent letters to Valeant, Turing, Retrophin Inc. and Rodelis Therapeutics asking about why they raised prices on drugs. The committee’s leaders, Senator Susan Collins of Maine, a Republican, and Senator Claire McCaskill of Missouri, a Democrat, said they would hold a hearing on the issue Dec. 9.

Endo Pharmaceuticals Inc., a subsidiary of Endo Health Solutions Inc. A determination that the non-crush-resistant OPANA ER was discontinued from sale for reasons of safety when not taken as prescribed

Clearwater doctor arrested on prescription drug charges

Times staff

Tuesday, December 2, 2014 10:37am


 
 
 Facebook

{Print this Story}Print

CLEARWATER — A pain management doctor was arrested Monday evening on charges that she bought controlled substances by using fraudulent prescriptions.




According to the Pinellas County Sheriff's Office, Dr. Lynne C. Columbus filled the prescriptions at several pharmacies in Pinellas.

Deputies arrested her at her practice, Gulf Coast Pain Management, at 3001 Eastland Blvd. in unincorporated Clearwater.

The investigation began last month when detectives received a tip about Columbus writing prescriptions for oxycodone using patient's names.

Columbus, 50, faces charges of attempting to obtain controlled substances by fraud.

She was booked into the Pinellas County jail, but was released Monday night on $10,000 bail.

Our Vision. Our Future.
Terrence Terifay

As President Mark Trudeau said at February's employee summit, Pharmaceuticals needs to tell a growth story to attract potential investors and analysts as we prepare for our separation in 16 months. Spin-Off Spotlight: Leadership Scoredcard


With approximately 20 different - and uniquely complex - specific areas of work (work streams) for the spin-off of Pharmaceuticals, Covidien's Board of Directors has developed a scorecard to simplify tracking of overall progress. The report organizes preparations into five core work streams; it previously included a sixth for hiring a new Pharmaceuticals President, but the recent arrival of Mark Trudeau completed that task. Read more ...<http://pulse/SiteDirectory/Pharma/News/featurednews/Pages/Spin-OffSpotlightLeadershipScorecard.aspx>

[cid:image024.jpg@01CCFAF6.11E28B20]
OptivantageTM with Simultaneous Injection Upgrade Meets Client Needs in EMEA Market



To address emerging market trends in Europe, Middle East and Africa (EMEA) markets, Pharmaceuticals launched its simultaneous injection software upgrade for the Optivantage dual-head computed tomography contrast delivery system to EMEA markets at ECR 2012, the annual meeting for the European Congress of Radiology, March 1-5, in Vienna, Austria. Customer feedback drove the development of the updated software. [cid:image024.jpg@01CCFAF6.11E28B20]
Strong Performance Puts Specialty Pharmaceuticals 'In the Black'



Almost two years since the launch of EXALGO(r) (hydromorphone HCI) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) and PENNSAID(r) (diclofenac sodium topical solution) 1.5% w/w, Specialty Pharmaceuticals has seen achievements across all functions, leading to financial success for the business. The financial term, "in the black" means that the business is profitable, as opposed to "in the red," which means it is operating at a loss. Read more ...<http://pulse/SiteDirectory/Pharma/News/featurednews/Pages/StrongQ1PerformancePutsSpecialtyPharmaceuticals%E2%80%98IntheBlack%E2%80%99.aspx>

[cid:image024.jpg@01CCFAF6.11E28B20]

The application deadline for the program is Friday, March 16. [cid:image024.jpg@01CCFAF6.11E28B20]
C.A.R.E.S. Alliance Convenes Panel on Prescription Drug Abuse; Shares Best Practices with Anti-drug Leaders and National Advocacy Groups

The C.A.R.E.S. AllianceSM in February shared its collaborative approach with more than 50 influential community leaders at the Community Anti-Drug Coalitions of America National Forum in National Harbor, Maryland. In a panel titled "Educate. Collaborate. Innovate," Panelists discussed the role of collaboration in overcoming prescription drug abuse, and best practices and recommendations for addressing this public health issue. Subject: Hydrocodone Scheduling - Financial risk to the Strategic Plan Forecasts

We have been asked to provide some guidance to management on the potential financial impact of the rescheduling of hydrocodone.
We can see three potential areas

1.       API hydrocodone sales/income

2.       Generic hydrocodone/APAP sales/income

3.       Zircon

What do we know:

1.       FDA has scheduled an advisory cmte meeting on October 29-30th

2.       20% of hydrocodone/APAP TRx are refilled prescriptions

3.       9% of hydrocodone/APAP TRx are written by physicians who do not write CII products

What do we suspect timing around re-scheduling based on advisory cmte action

1.       Advisory cmtes have taken between 6-9 months to come to a conclusion/report

2.       Further add DEA action and time to implement   would not expect rescheduling to occur before June 2013 and most likely January 2014

What will be the issues:

1.        Number on logistical issue will be sufficient vault space and the time it takes to acquire/build vault space   could also impact manufacturers

2.       Warehousing chains and other direct purchasers of CIII products will most likely not have vault capacity or insufficient vault capacity and will require wholesalers to provide on a just in time basis.

3.       Retail pharmacies will have insufficient vault space and will either be out of stock more often

Based on the above would like to get some sense of downsides and potential upsides (codeine sales for instance)

Need to get this by end of the week
Have met with the API and Generics folks to start process
Brands   let me know how I can facilitate
David

From: Danette Kadlic <dkadlic@fingerpaintmarketing.com>

    Anne Marie White <awhite@fingerpaintmarketing.com>


Hi Mike & DJ - 


Hope this note finds you well. Attached, please find a VERY ROUGH draft of the sales force training slides for the patient experience program. The team from PI provided the templated content and I just went through and cleaned it up very quickly to drop in our program name, the brand name, and a couple of other details. Please note that there are still some placeholders in here that I've highlighted in red that we are waiting on. I would like for our team to take another pass at cleaning this up once we get through the big push for our PARC submissions, but I didn't want to delay any more in getting this over to you. 


Additionally, here are some additional details that PI has provided for the role playing exercise. Please have a look and let me know if this will work for your needs or if you would like us to make any adjustments. If you are good with this text below, then we will use this as a foundation to the Sales Force Instruction Sheet that will accompany the delivery of the program materials when they are shipped to the representatives. 


The Patient Prescription Insights program provides feedback about XARTEMIS XR to doctors, through the voice of their own patients.

 

Key points:

1.       A great way to get quick feedback on how your patients feel about this new treatment option

2.       Patients value both the copay savings as well as the opportunity to give you feedback

3.       [Referring to sample report] This is an example of the kind of input you ll get from your own patients

4.       No extra work is required   simply give your patients the Kit with the prescription and we take care of the rest

 

Steps:

Introduce the Program by closing your detail with an introduction of the XARTEMIS XR Patient Prescription Insights Program and drop off <5?> patient kits.
Gain Commitment from the doctor and office staff to participate in the program and invite eligible patients to enroll in the Program.
Return <One Week> Later and encourage the doctor to give a patient kit to patients who receive a script for XARTEMIS XR.
Return again and continue to encourage the doctor to give the patient kits to patients who receive a script for XARTEMIS XR.

 

How it works:

         At the end of your sales call, you will introduce the program to your Healthcare Professional and drop off the kits

         Doctors will be automatically enrolled in the program via a data feed from your <SFA> system after you drop off the kits.

         Doctors will receive a welcome letter with a sample report to remind them about the program.

         The patient is provided the XARTEMIS XR Starter Kit along with their script. It contains specific enrollment directions

         Patients enroll in the survey and complete the survey online or on the phone. Surveys assess treatment experience and satisfaction

         Doctors receive a report of their patient s responses to the surveys

Benefits for you:

         Positively impacts your sales by establishing your credibility and interest in promoting patient education and communication between patient and Healthcare Professional

         Provides an effective tool to impact prescribing behavior among Healthcare Professionals in your territory by creating brand impressions even when you aren t detailing them

         Creates an opportunity to reach Healthcare Professionals and encourage them to prescribe XARTEMIS XR and see what their patients  experiences are.

Your role:

         Close your detail with the program flashcard, and leave it with the office.

         Encourage Healthcare Professionals to give their patients a XARTEMIS XR Starter Kit that s all they have to do

         Follow up with offices to keep the program top of mind!

Benefits for Healthcare Professionals:

To: "Courtney Cox (courtneyc@moorecommgroup.com)" <courtneyc@moorecommgroup.com>


Courtney,

 

See comments by Mark Tyndall on page 2 (Key Message).  Can you change the following paragraph to read:

 

Prescription drugs and other medicines that are no longer needed often remain in your medicine cabinet or other locations in your home. In the past, it was recommended to flush these medications down the toilet or sink   but we now know that drugs that are disposed by flushing can enter the environment, and may have an effect on as well as cause harm to fish and other aquatic life.

 

Also, on Page 3, Derek wants to make sure that this is still the  fastest-growing and deadliest public safety issue  for AG Bondi.  Derek s perspective is that the state leadership is declaring victory and that it s getting better.  Can you just make sure that this is still a true statement?

 

Prescription drug misuse is Florida s  fastest-growing and deadliest public safety issue  according to Attorney General Pam Bondi s Prescription Drug Diversion and Abuse Roadmap. Florida has taken the first step to effectively address prescription drug abuse with the pill mill crackdown and enactment of the Prescription Drug Monitoring Program, but a comprehensive strategy is necessary.

 

Thanks.

Kevin

Attached is the final version of the media tool kit and press release for this Saturday s kick-off event of the CADCA lead drug take-back and opioid disposal research project.

 

As a reminder, Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals is sponsoring the project which seeks to determine what type of public awareness messaging is most effective in driving change in an individual s behavior regarding safe use, storage and disposal of prescription drugs   messaging regarding their own, or family safety; safeguarding the community; or protecting the environment.  Mallinckrodt is also donating 40,000 of the medication inactivation pouches.

 

The kick-off takes place this Saturday, September 26 simultaneously in four Florida communities, with the local dignitaries speaking at the Tampa event.  The media kit will go out in advance   ideally tomorrow.  Moore Communications in Florida is handling all media/communications for the event.

Good morning,

 

A good friend of mine just sent me this proposed bill that came to them from the Federal Director of Government Affairs @ HDMA.    When you read the bill, the seizure piece is a no brainer and the reclassification of the Hydro apap from a CIII to a CII makes a lot of sense as well.    I wonder if our competitors are positioned to move their CIII’s to a CII vault like we are???
