-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------

To: Federal Government Affairs Committee and Regulatory Affairs Committee

 

Last week, Congressman Vern Buchanan (R-FL) introduced the “Pill Mill Crackdown Act of 2011” (H.R. 1065) which includes provisions to support state-based prescription drug monitoring programs; use the money from seized illicit operations for drug treatment; strengthen prescription standards for certain addictive pain drugs; and toughen prison terms and fines for pill mill operators. I have attached a copy of the bill, which was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and House Energy and Commerce Committee.

 

According to the Congressman’s press release, the bill would:

·         Toughen federal penalties for pill mill operators by doubling the prison sentence from 10 to 20 years and tripling the fine from $1 million to $3 million.

·         Stipulate that assets seized from violators be used to: fund drug monitoring databases in the states; fund DEA enforcement actions against Pill Mills; and, support drug treatment programs within the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration. The DEA last month seized an estimated $2.5 million in illicit assets owned by pill mill owners in South Florida.

·         Reclassify hydrocodone combination drugs (one of the most addictive and dangerous drug mixtures) to make them a Schedule II drug that is more difficult to prescribe and obtain.

We have just heard that Ontario is considering to list Methadose on June 1st with a possible roll-out of 30 days before delisting the compounded product. The date is still tentative as Ontario is going through some political changes, but we are hopeful that it will be met.

 

By chance, the Ontario Pharmacists Association is holding its annual meeting (June 19th-June 21st), ie during this transition period. OPA could collaborate with Mallinckrodt in order to have a lunch and learn about the transition from compounded methadone to Methadose – we were thinking about having Dr Beth Sproule for this event: she is the leading individual who took part in the guidelines update for the introduction of Methadose in Ontario.

 

OPA would need some financial support from Mallinckrodt to host this event – about $15,000. It would be a unique opportunity to reach a large number of pharmacists and educate them on how to use Methadose according to the new guidelines. It would also be a great opportunity for Medical Affairs to connect with KOLs in Ontario. Unfortunately, this event was unplanned and Marketing does not have the budget to support it.

 

Please let me know if Medical Affairs would be able to provide the required financial support – we could then coordinate with OPA and KOLs.

 

 

There is also another opportunity in British Columbia, where the transition took place in February. London Drugs (largest pharmacy chain in BC) will hold its annual conference in June – we could support a speaker presentation on Saturday May 31st, given by a doctor specialist who will discuss MMT in BC. They allow 45 minutes for the presentation including a 5 minute question and answer period. Attendance is approximately 180 staff London Drugs pharmacists, coming from Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and British Columbia. London Drugs covers all expenses for the staff. Due to the costs of this event, they charge $ 3,500 to participate to the company. The vendor pays the speaker honorarium and also finds the speaker.

 

Please let me know at your earliest convenience if this could be of interest to Medical Affairs.

Subject: EXALGO Monitoring Report -- Week of 5/21



 

Hi team,

 

Below please find this week s monitoring report for EXALGO; this report includes coverage from Friday, May 14, to Friday, May 21, 2010.

 

This week, RecoveryView.com published an editorial about EXALGO, citing its concerns for the potential abuse and misuse of the medication. The article begins by highlighting the evolution in pain management from Oxycontin, a 12-hour formula for pain management, to EXALGO, which is taken every 24 hours. The reporter s concerns with the drug is that opiate-na ve patients are at high-risk for overdosing on EXALGO, and that there may be a greater possibility for people to divert the drug for illegal sale. The reporter did have hope that, with proper patient and prescriber education, the drug will be used to effectively treat opioid-tolerant patients who suffer from moderate to severe chronic pain.

 

Of other interest this week: A conversation about EXALGO was posted on the CafePharma forum titled,  Five reasons why EXALGO ER is a failure.  The forum post highlighted the top-five reasons one member felt EXALGO was not going to be successful, including the price of the medication and the potential risks involved with taking EXALGO. One person replied to the forum claiming to be a representative from Covidien, accusing the person who began the discussion of being an employee of a competitor.

 

The Los Angeles Times wrote a blog post this week about an essay published in the past issue of the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA). The essay was written by a medical researcher who made headlines last year when his fianc e died after the two injected themselves with a narcotic buprenorphine. The author of the essay became addicted to opioids, marijuana and other drugs while studying the effects of drugs on the brain for the University of Maryland. The author is quoted in the blog post as saying that,   when it comes to drug use, the perception of control is really nothing more than an illusion. 

 

Finally, Fierce Pharma Manufacturing posted an article this week that listed tips on creating a successful REMS program. The article highlighted three tips from REMS experts on making a successful program: start creating your REMS program early, do your user and product homework, engage your users and stockholders to line up potential resources.

Message from Steve Carchedi

President, Commercial Operations   North America

 
 

 

MNK-795 File Accepted for Priority Review

New Drug Application marks our first application as Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals

 

<image009.jpg>Today we announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has accepted the New Drug Application for MNK-795 and granted it Priority Review.  As you are aware, MNK-795 is an important component of our growth story at Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals and today marks a significant milestone for all of us.

 

MNK-795 is controlled-release oral formulation of oxycodone and acetaminophen that has been studied for the management of moderate to severe acute pain where the use of an opioid analgesic is appropriate and will be part our Brands product line.  MNK-795 was developed by our Research and Development (R&D) team using two known compounds and incorporates technology designed to provide abuse deterrence and tamper resistance.

 

Based on certain qualities of MNK-795, the FDA granted a Priority Review, a designation given to drugs that, if approved, offer significant improvements in the safety or effectiveness of the treatment when compared to standard applications.  As a result of this classification, the product will be reviewed faster than a Standard Review, and if approved could allow us to bring this product to market earlier to help treat patients in pain.

 

The successful filing acceptance and Priority Review are a result of the hard work and dedication of employees across the organization, specifically in the R&D, Regulatory, Commercial, Operations, Legal, and Medical Affairs teams.  Thank you to all employees who got us to this point.

 

Our next milestone as an organization will be at PAINWeek September 4-7, where we will share our clinical data for MNK-795 with attending healthcare providers.  This will be a great opportunity for us to share the clinical story of our exciting product.

 

Look for more information on our @work intranet as we approach the FDA decision date and (if approved) launch to learn more about the teams working across the organization supporting this important product.

 

?   PLEASE CLICK HERE OR READ BELOW FOR THE FULL PRESS RELEASE.

 

 

 
MALLINCKRODT NEW DRUG APPLICATION GRANTED PRIORITY REVIEW BY FDA

 

Mallinckrodt s MNK-795   controlled-release oxycodone/acetaminophen combination

accepted for filing by U.S. Food and Drug Administration

 

 

Hazelwood, MO   July 29, 2013   Mallinckrodt (NYSE: MNK) today announced that the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has accepted for filing the New Drug Application (NDA) for MNK-795 and granted priority review. MNK-795 is a controlled-release oral formulation of oxycodone and acetaminophen that has been studied for the management of moderate to severe acute pain where the use of an opioid analgesic is appropriate. FDA priority review is a defined NDA review process used for drugs that, if approved, offer significant improvements in the safety or effectiveness of the treatment when compared to standard applications. 

 

If approved, MNK-795 would be a controlled-release oxycodone and acetaminophen combination medication that has immediate and extended release components. The dosage form was designed using Depomed s advanced Acuform  drug delivery technology with tamper-resistant properties.

 

 Despite the number of available pain medications, patients continue to experience unresolved pain and lack treatment options that offer fast-acting and long-lasting relief. We are pleased the FDA granted priority review designation,  said Mark Trudeau, President and Chief Executive Officer, Mallinckrodt Pharmaceuticals.   Mallinckrodt has unique capabilities in complex formulations such as MNK-795 and this marks an important milestone for us as our first NDA acceptance as an independent specialty pharmaceutical company.     

 

Mallinckrodt s submission is based on data from a comprehensive clinical trial program for MNK-795 that included 14 clinical studies with 1,281 patients. The studies evaluated pharmacokinetics, efficacy, safety and abuse liability. 

 

 

About Mallinckrodt

Mallinckrodt is a leading global specialty pharmaceuticals business that develops, manufactures, markets and distributes specialty pharmaceutical products and medical imaging agents. The company s Specialty Pharmaceuticals segment includes branded and generic drugs, and the Global Medical Imaging segment includes contrast media and nuclear imaging agents. Mallinckrodt has approximately 5,500 employees worldwide with direct sales in roughly 50 countries and distribution in approximately 40 countries. The company s 2012 revenue totaled $2.1 billion. To learn more about Mallinckrodt, visit www.mallinckrodt.com.

[RxNews] NY State Doctor charged with selling CS RX's with no exam

a aroneck doctor char • ed with sellin
controlled dru prescriptions with no exa
Sep 5 2013
2 Comments

•

Written by

Hoa Nguyen

Zoom
Martin Korn

More

MAMARONECK — A six-month undercover investigation has authorities accusing a town doctor with selling prescriptions
for Xanax and other controlled substances with little to no examination or consultation, the Westchester County district
attorney said.
Dr. Martin L. Korn, 61, of West Garden Road has been accused of spending less than 10 minutes with patients and failing
to acquire basic or essential clinical information from them, with his initial and follow-up assessments falling below
standards of medical practice, the district attorney said.
He was charged with three counts of criminal sale of a prescription for a controlled substance, a felony, and additional
charges are expected, officials said.
Undercover officers were able to purchase prescriptions from Korn and fulfill them in pharmacies across New York,
officials said.
The drugs Korn is accused of selling are clonazepam, lorazepam, zaleplon, Lunesta, Adderall, zolpidem, Oxycontin,
oxycodone, diazepam, Xanax, Ritalin, Ambien and Valium, authorities said.
Korn, who has been arraigned, is expected to appear Monday in Mamaroneck Town Court.
He faces a maximum sentence of 15 years in state prison on each count.
Officials also have moved to bar him from writing prescriptions for controlled substances pending the outcome of a
hearing.

MNKOI 0001120030

 Korn has a practice at his home with his wife, Dr. Ada Korn, a clinical psychologist. Officials at the District Attorney's
Office said they do not believe she had any role in her husband's alleged wrongdoing.
Reached by email Thursday evening, Martin Korn declined to comment on the charges, noting that he would have to
speak to his attorney.
In addition to the district attorney, a U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration task force including state police and county
officers from Westchester and Rockland participated in the investigation.

> I had the same exact thought as you. I have been talking with folks regarding the importance of  Communications  and how this vehicle / function could operate.  I think we have an opportunity to organize, channel and lead communications to field that should exist beyond email.  We could incorporate a more formal process via an electronic distribution.  I believe we could create a series of communication buckets (eg, cover letter templates in a branded memo format) that could allow greater control and more importantly greater receipt/retention by our target audience (field sales).  The communication buckets could be as follows:
>

We had messages from each product team with important competitive updates, from Ryan on the Fast Start Contest, from Jamie on the  Spin  and then an update on Pennsaid samples and the FDA. > 
> Diane, if you have any suggestions on pacing these communications more effectively I think that there would be tremendous benefit for improved readership.

> Thanks
> Ron
> 
> From: Kast, Mike
> Sent: Tuesday, December 20, 2011 4:13 PM
> To: #MKG - Pharma Field Sales; #MKG - Dos Prod - RSDs; #MKG - Dos Prod - DMs (Brand); #MKG - Dos Prod - CAMs (Brand)
> Cc: Harrell, Jamie; Terifay, Terry W; Novak, Rod P; Webb, Kevin J; Lierman, Jennifer A; Patterson, Mike E; Wessler, Michael; Rausch, Ryan; Wickline, Ronald P; Swartz, Betty Jean (BJ); Jones, Jason D
> Subject: Competitive Update - Vimovo and Duexis
> 
> Field Sales Force-
> 
> There have been a few recent changes in the NSAID market. The PENNSAID Brand Team wanted to provide you with an update so you are knowledgeable about our competition and what your customers may be hearing.
> 
> Vimovo 
> The FDA recently issued a class wide warning for all Proton Pump Inhibitors (PPIs) for bone fracture. There is evidence to suggest that chronic PPI use is associated with osteoporosis related fractures of the hip, wrist, and spine. The warning cautions that PPIs should be taken at the lowest dose for shortest duration possible to reduce this risk. Vimovo contains esomeprazole (a PPI) and as a result a warning on bone fracture has recently been placed in the Vimovo PI. Also, since Vimovo has esomeprazole in combination with naproxen (an NSAID), and is indicated for 2 tablets daily in the treatment of chronic conditions. Please see the top of page 11 of the attached Vimovo PI for more information on this new warning.
> 
> Additionally, as a result of containing esomeprazole, Vimovo has another warning. This additional warning is for hypomagnesemia, or low magnesium levels, seen with chronic use of PPIs. Serious adverse events that can result from hypomagnesemia include  arrhythmias and seizures. Please see the top of page 12 of the attached Vimovo PI for more information on this warning.
> 
> While Vimovo does an effective job of reducing GI risk from taking oral naproxen alone, it has not been shown to reduce other risks associated with NSAIDs such as abnormal liver function tests, cardiovascular risks, or renal risks, and introduces other risks associated with PPIs.  As a reminder, while PENNSAID is an NSAID and carries the same black box warning, as a topical it produces < 1% of the peak plasma concentration compared to oral NSAIDs.  In addition, topical NSAIDs carry neither the bone fracture or hypomagnesemia warnings, even with chronic use.
> 
> Duexis 
> 
> Late last week, Horizon Pharmaceuticals announced the licensure of Duexis, a combination NSAID containing ibuprofen and famotidine (a histamine H2-receptor antagonist). You may be more familiar with famotidine from its brand name, Pepcid .
> 
> 
> 
> While Duexis is the combination of two products that are both currently available over the counter, the precise dose (800 mg ibuprofen and 26.6 mg famotidine) is not available over the counter in one pill.  In addition, the product is dosed TID. Please see the attached Duexis PI for more information.
> 
> Because Duexis contains an H-2 antagonist as opposed to a PPI, it does not contain the bone fracture or hypomagnesemia warnings. But similar to the PPI in Vimovo, the H-2 antagonist in Duexis only addresses the GI adverse events; not any of the other NSAID associated risks such as abnormal liver function tests, cardiovascular risks, or renal risks.
> 
> Going Forward
> These two market changes are certainly interesting, but they should not change your approach to PENNSAID. Do not let this distract you from the messaging you learned at the National Sales Meeting.  Our message and strategy are strong   for some high risk patients as identified by the physician who cannot tolerate an oral NSAID, some of these patients may have limited treatment options (even with a combination oral NSAID), PENNSAID may be a viable treatment option. As a result, the STRATEGY, LOGIC, and MESSAGE you learned in Dallas are still your best option!
>

   INDICATION
EXALGO (hydromorphone HCl) Extended-Release Tablets (CII) is indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION 

WARNING: ABUSE POTENTIAL, LIFE-THREATENING RESPIRATORY DEPRESSION, and ACCIDENTAL EXPOSURE
Abuse Potential
EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. Assess each patient s risk for opioid abuse or addiction prior to prescribing EXALGO. The risk for opioid abuse is increased in patients with a personal or family history of substance abuse (including drug or alcohol abuse or addiction) or mental illness (e.g., major depressive disorder). Routinely monitor all patients receiving EXALGO for signs of misuse, abuse, and addiction during treatment.
Life-threatening Respiratory Depression
Respiratory depression, including fatal cases, may occur with use of EXALGO, even when the drug has been used as recommended and not misused or abused. EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only. Proper dosing and titration are essential and EXALGO should be prescribed only by healthcare professionals who are knowledgeable in the use of potent opioids for the management of chronic pain. Monitor for respiratory depression, especially during initiation of EXALGO or following a dose increase. Crushing, dissolving, or chewing the tablet can cause rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.
Accidental Exposure
Accidental ingestion of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone. 


CONTRAINDICATIONS 
   EXALGO is contraindicated in: 
  - Opioid non-tolerant patients. Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant. 
  - Patients with significant respiratory depression 
  - Patients with acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting or in the absence of resuscitative equipment 
  - Patients with known or suspected paralytic ileus 
  - Patients who have had surgical procedures and/or underlying disease resulting in narrowing of the gastrointestinal tract, or have  blind loops  of the gastrointestinal tract or gastrointestinal obstruction 
  - Patients with hypersensitivity (e.g., anaphylaxis) to hydromorphone or sulfite-containing medications 
   EXALGO is indicated for opioid tolerant patients only. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer. 
   EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic and is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain. It is contraindicated in patients who need management of mild pain or pain not expected to persist. 
   Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery. 
   Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO. 
   Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison s disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment. 
   Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO. 
   Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness. Post marketing events include hypersensitivity reactions, angioedema and urticaria. 
   Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible to intracranial effects of CO2 retention. 
   Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO.

From: PCMA SmartBrief <pcma@smartbrief.com>
Date: Mon, 26 Sep 2016 15:39:19 +0000
To: bonnie.new@mallinckrodt.com


PCMA suggests ways to reduce opioid abuse, lower drug prices | PCMA: MAC lists help payers keep drug prices under control | Amgen's biosimilar of AbbVie's Humira gets FDA approval
 
Created for bonnie.new@mallinckrodt.com |  Web Version 

 
 
 September 26, 2016 

 FOLLOW PCMA ON TWITTER    {Twitter} 

 

 
{PCMA SmartBrief} {PCMA SmartBrief} 

 
News for the PBM Industry SIGN UP ⋅   FORWARD ⋅   ARCHIVE 

 

 

Featured Stories 

 


PCMA suggests ways to reduce opioid abuse, lower drug prices Testifying at a House hearing, Pharmaceutical Care Management Association President and CEO Mark Merritt said Congress should direct the FDA to prioritize approval of drugs with little or no competition, eliminate barriers to value-based pricing arrangements, eliminate protected drug classes under Medicare Part D, require clinicians to e-prescribe controlled substances, and require states to improve accessibility and interoperability of prescription drug monitoring databases.
MedPage Today (free registration) (9/23)  {LinkedIn}{LinkedIn} {Twitter}{Twitter} {Facebook}{Facebook} {Google+}{Google+} {Email}{Email}





PCMA: MAC lists help payers keep drug prices under control Pharmaceutical industry consolidation and drug shortages have led to higher-than-expected prices on some generic drugs, but maximum allowable cost lists help payers keep prices under control, says Pharmaceutical Care Management Association spokesman Charles Cote.
Bloomberg BNA (subscription required) (9/22)  {LinkedIn}{LinkedIn} {Twitter}{Twitter} {Facebook}{Facebook} {Google+}{Google+} {Email}{Email}




 

 

Legislative & Regulatory News 

 


Amgen's biosimilar of AbbVie's Humira gets FDA approval Amgen's Amjevita, or adalimumab-atto, a biosimilar version of AbbVie's anti-inflammatory drug Humira, has been approved by the FDA to treat conditions including psoriatic arthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriasis and Crohn's disease. The drug is the fourth biosimilar approved by the agency.
The Wall Street Journal (tiered subscription model) (9/23),  Reuters (9/23)  {LinkedIn}{LinkedIn} {Twitter}{Twitter} {Facebook}{Facebook} {Google+}{Google+} {Email}{Email}





States say drugmaker thwarted generics of anti-addiction drug A lawsuit by 35 states and the District of Columbia says that drugmaker Indivior conspired with MonoSol Rx to keep generic versions of Indivior's Suboxone tablets off the market. The drug is used to treat opioid addiction, and the plaintiffs say Indivior developed an oral strip version to maintain market exclusivity.
Reuters (9/22)  {LinkedIn}{LinkedIn} {Twitter}{Twitter} {Facebook}{Facebook} {Google+}{Google+} {Email}{Email}





Co-ops' failures affecting individual health plan market The downfall of all but a handful of 23 nonprofit insurers created through the Affordable Care Act changed the risk pools in commercial plans remaining in the individual market, analysts say.
Bloomberg (9/23)  {LinkedIn}{LinkedIn} {Twitter}{Twitter} {Facebook}{Facebook} {Google+}{Google+} {Email}{Email}





BCBS exits Neb. ACA exchange business Blue Cross Blue Shield of Nebraska will not offer health plans for 2017 on the state's Affordable Care Act exchange but will continue to offer individual plans directly or through licensed agents, according to a company statement.
KETV-TV (Omaha, Neb.) (9/23)  {LinkedIn}{LinkedIn} {Twitter}{Twitter} {Facebook}{Facebook} {Google+}{Google+} {Email}{Email}





US faces prospect of government shutdown Without passing a continuing resolution, the federal government could face a shutdown this week. Disagreements remain over a proposed funding bill, including its lack of funding to address water contamination in Flint, Mich.

Dear Pharmacist:

You are probably aware of the shortage and potential supply disruption in certain extended release opioids. This may present a challenge for you, the physicians you work with, and your patients. However, your opioid-tolerant patients with chronic pain may have another treatment option.

STOCK EXALGO TODAY
Now is the time to make sure you are stocked with EXALGO, a once-daily opioid that your physicians may be prescribing for their opioid-tolerant patients.

READILY AVAILABLE WITH FAVORABLE COVERAGE
EXALGO is covered for 8 out of 10 managed care patients without prior authorization. Additionally, the EXALGO co-pay discount card<http://whatcounts.jobson.com/t?r=4&c=0&l=3818&ctl=46EC0:733B4C71B177CE918D50631244195C66&> reduces the co-pay of each eligible prescription by up to $60, making EXALGO an affordable choice for most patients.

Fingertip Formulary data accessed 7/6/2011. Medicaid plans not included in data.


[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15839Covidien(Exalgo)PH_LG/wv4/images/54478_covexa_e_pharm_alert2_lo20_04.jpg]


QUESTIONS?
If you have any questions regarding EXALGO, visit www.EXALGO.com<http://whatcounts.jobson.com/t?r=4&c=0&l=3818&ctl=22B1C:733B4C71B177CE918D50631244195C66&> or contact Covidien at 1-800-778-7898.
Please click here for Full Prescribing Information<http://whatcounts.jobson.com/t?r=4&c=0&l=3818&ctl=22AED:733B4C71B177CE918D50631244195C66&>.

INDICATION
EXALGO is an extended-release oral formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients requiring continuous, around-the-clock opioid analgesia for an extended period of time.

IMPORTANT RISK INFORMATION
[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15839Covidien(Exalgo)PH_LG/wv4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_06t.jpg][http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15839Covidien(Exalgo)PH_LG/wv4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_06m.jpg]

[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15839Covidien(Exalgo)PH_LG/wv4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_07.jpg]


WARNING: POTENTIAL FOR ABUSE, IMPORTANCE OF
PROPER PATIENT SELECTION AND LIMITATIONS OF USE

Potential for Abuse
EXALGO contains hydromorphone, an opioid agonist and a Schedule II controlled substance with an abuse liability similar to other opioid analgesics. EXALGO can be abused in a manner similar to other opioid agonists, legal or illicit. These risks should be considered when administering, prescribing, or dispensing EXALGO in situations where the healthcare professional is concerned about increased risk of misuse, abuse, or diversion. Schedule II opioid substances which include hydromorphone, morphine, oxycodone, fentanyl, oxymorphone and methadone have the highest potential for abuse and risk of fatal overdose due to respiratory depression.

Proper Patient Selection
EXALGO is an extended-release formulation of hydromorphone hydrochloride indicated for the management of moderate to severe pain in opioid tolerant patients when a continuous around-the-clock opioid analgesic is needed for an extended period of time. Patients considered opioid tolerant are those who are taking at least 60 mg oral morphine per day, 25 mcg transdermal fentanyl/hour, 30 mg oral oxycodone/day, 8 mg oral hydromorphone/day, 25 mg oral oxymorphone/day or an equianalgesic dose of another opioid, for a week or longer.
EXALGO is for use in opioid tolerant patients only.
Fatal respiratory depression could occur in patients who are not opioid tolerant.
Accidental consumption of EXALGO, especially in children, can result in a fatal overdose of hydromorphone.

Limitations of Use
EXALGO is not indicated for the management of acute or postoperative pain.
EXALGO is not intended for use as an as-needed analgesic.
EXALGO tablets are to be swallowed whole and are not to be broken, chewed, dissolved, crushed or injected. Taking broken, chewed, dissolved or crushed EXALGO or its contents leads to rapid release and absorption of a potentially fatal dose of hydromorphone.




[http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15839Covidien(Exalgo)PH_LG/wv4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_08t.jpg][http://www.alertmarketing.com/email/JHCE/15839Covidien(Exalgo)PH_LG/wv4/images/54477_covexa_e_md_alert2_lo8_08m.jpg]



*


EXALGO is also contraindicated in patients who:
- need management of mild pain or pain not expected
  to persist
- have significant impaired respiratory function including
  those with acute or severe bronchial asthma or hypercarbia
- have or are suspected to have paralytic ileus
- have narrowed or obstructed gastrointestinal tract
  including those from previous surgery or "blind loops"
  in the GI tract
- have known hypersensitivity to any components including
  hydromorphone hydrochloride and sulfites


*


Avoid concurrent use of alcohol and EXALGO. Concurrent use of EXALGO with CNS depressants, including alcohol, increases risk of respiratory depression, hypotension, and profound sedation, potentially resulting in coma or death. EXALGO may impair the ability to drive a car or operate machinery.


*


Not intended in patients who have received MAO inhibitors within 14 days of starting EXALGO.


*


Use with caution and in reduced doses in older or debilitated patients, as well as patients with renal or hepatic insufficiency, Addison's disease, delirium tremens, myxedema or hypothyroidism, prostatic hypertrophy or urethral stricture, toxic psychosis. May aggravate convulsions in patients with convulsive disorders; may induce or aggravate seizures in some clinical settings. Consider use of an alternate analgesic in patients with severe renal impairment.


*


Respiratory depression, which occurs more frequently in elderly or debilitated patients, is the chief hazard with EXALGO.


*


Serious adverse events could also include hypotensive effects, GI effects, cardiac arrest from overdose and precipitation of withdrawal. Most common adverse events (>10%) seen in clinical studies (N=2474) were: constipation (31%), nausea (28%), vomiting, somnolence, headache, asthenia and dizziness.


*


Use EXALGO with extreme caution in patients susceptible
to intracranial effects of CO2 retention.


*


Do not abruptly discontinue EXALGO

Re:  PENNSAID shift from 1.5% to 2%

 

Please take a look at the attached   the shift from 1.5% ~10K TRx s/month to 2% ~2K TRx s/month presents significant issues for SICP:  to prevent absolute IC $ from declining due to PENNSAID mix shift, IC $ / TRx must increase while moderating for the issue created in previous SICP plans:  compensating same $ payout / TRx for low volume territories same as high volume territories.

Subject: IC Proposals



 

Stacy,

 

The attached slide deck illustrates a few comp plans that we worked with ZS to model. Slide 1 shows a comparison between a $50/$100 graduated commission above goal (which we looked at Friday), as well as the straight $100 commission rate above goal (proposed today). Looking at the comparison, the payouts are slightly better, but still shows a bias towards lower payment for lower volume territories.

 

Neal and I had an opportunity to discuss this with Jay today and came up with an alternative plan that would pay the current payout curve up to 125%, at which point a $100 commission rate per TRx would kick in. By extending the payout curve to 125% instead of 100%, we are able to help provide a little additional value for the first couple scripts above goal to the lower volume territories. This approach helps reduce the bias created by a straight commission rate at 100%.

 

Additionally, ZS has come up with a plan that pays out according to the current payout curve, but applies a soft cap of  no more than $150 per TRx . According to this methodology, the value per percentage point will be normalized to $150/TRx if the value were otherwise greater. This plan is very similar to the plan outlined above, except that the point at which a commission will kick in is variable depending on the size of the goal. If the goal is small (37 or less, which will likely be the majority of territories for 2%), the commission will kick in at the first incremental script above goal. If the goal is larger than 37, the rep will earn a lower amount per script until the commission kicks in.

 

The approaches are very similar. Looking at the analysis on the attached slides (slide 2), the variance between the methods is small. The first approach provides a little more value up front, while the second approach spreads it out a bit. If we adjust the commission rate and the soft cap to be the same, the variation above 150% in the second model (goal of 16) would be even less.

 

Please review the slides and information and let me know if you have any questions or comments. If you re still available in the morning, we can touch base on the phone to discuss these options.

Title


Effect of i.v. acetaminophen on total hip or knee replacement surgery: A case-matched evaluation of a national patient database.


Source


American Journal of Health-System Pharmacy. 72(22):1961-8, 2015 Nov 15.


Country of Publication


United States


Abstract


PURPOSE: The effects of i.v. acetaminophen on adverse events, hospital length of stay (LOS), and overall hospital costs for total hip or knee replacements were evaluated.
METHODS: We conducted a matched-pairs analysis of adult inpatients who underwent elective total hip arthroplasty or total knee arthroplasty in hospitals participating in the Premier Healthcare Alliance from January 1, 2011, to November 30, 2012. Each case who received i.v. acetaminophen on the day of surgery was matched to a control who did not receive i.v. acetaminophen within the same hospital. Treatment groups were analyzed for differences in the rate of adverse effects, LOS, and hospital resource utilization.
RESULTS: A total of 22,146 cases and controls were similar in terms of age, race, sex, marital status, insurance status, and preoperative comorbidities. Overall adverse events were significantly lower with i.v. acetaminophen (24.3%) than with controls (26.3%, p < 0.001), numerically less frequent in all subgroups, and significantly less frequent for renal, infectious, and miscellaneous adverse events (all p < 0.05). I.V. acetaminophen was also associated with a shorter LOS, with 1 out of 11 patients discharged one day earlier (p < 0.001) and lower average hospital costs: $16,381 for cases compared with $16,927 for controls (p < 0.001). Cost savings estimated by structural equation modeling of $547 per patient were due to $325 from direct effects and $222 from indirect effects, the latter mediated through adverse events and reduced LOS.
CONCLUSION: In this retrospective cohort study of case-matched patients who underwent total hip or knee replacement surgery, multimodal analgesia with i.v. acetaminophen was associated with improved clinical outcomes in terms of fewer adverse events, shortened LOS, and reduced total hospital resources compared with patients who did not receive i.v. acetaminophen.Copyright © 2015 by the American Society of Health-System Pharmacists, Inc. All rights reserved.

Title


Comparison of preoperative oral acetazolamide and intraperitoneal normal saline irrigation for reduction of postoperative pain after laparoscopic cholecystectomy.


Source


Journal of Laparoendoscopic & Advanced Surgical Techniques. Part A. 25(4):285-90, 2015 Apr.


Country of Publication


United States


Abstract


PURPOSE: Visceral and shoulder tip pain following laparoscopic cholecystectomy is mainly due to carbon dioxide (CO2) insufflation. Various methods have been adopted to eliminate residual CO2. We compared the postoperative analgesic efficacy of intraperitoneal normal saline (30mL/kg) irrigation with preoperative oral acetazolamide administration in patients undergoing laparoscopic cholecystectomy.

MATERIALS AND METHODS: Sixty patients between 20 and 60 years of age were included in this prospective, randomized, double-blind study. Patients in Group I received placebo, Group II patients received preoperative oral acetazolamide (5mg/kg), and Group III patients received intraperitoneal irrigation with 30mL/kg of normal saline. Intravenous paracetamol (1g) was administered every 6 hours for postoperative analgesia. Parietal and visceral pain scores at rest, on movement, and on coughing and shoulder tip pain were recorded using a visual analog scale after arrival in the postanesthesia care unit, at 1, 2, 4, 6, 12, and 24 hours after surgery. Rescue analgesia was provided with an intravenous fentanyl (1mug/kg) bolus whenever the visual analog scale score was >4.

RESULTS: Compared with Group I, Group III patients had significantly lower visceral pain scores at all time intervals except at 12 hours. Group III patients also recorded significantly lower visceral pain scores than Group II from 2 to 24 hours. There was no significant difference in shoulder tip pain. The total dose of fentanyl used was significantly less in Group III.

CONCLUSIONS: Intraperitoneal normal saline irrigation is more effective than acetazolamide in reducing postoperative visceral pain after laparoscopic cholecystectomy and has significant opioid-sparing effect. However, its effect on shoulder pain is comparable to that of acetazolamide.

Subject: RE: ER/LA Class Safety Labeling Changes: EXALGO (NDA 021217/013)



 

Dear Lisa,

Please find attached Exalgo PI with FDA changes accepted and additional changes tracked.  Our global labeling group has edited the margins, spacing and footer to reflect the current revision, as well as replacing several instances of the infinity sign with a corrected symbol.  Two instances of EXALGO in all caps are also included as minor edits.

 

For the FDA comment to include increments in mg for dose increases, Mallinckrodt proposes to edit the revised text to replace 4 mg with 8 mg as the lowest available strength of EXALGO, for which multiples of the same strength could be prescribed until the patient was stabilized on a dose.  The rationale comment from the labeling is copied into this email for ease of reading.

 

               Comment as Rationale for Change from 4-mg to 8-mg Incremental Dose Increase:

The 4?mg dose increment is problematic from a prescription/patient instructions-logistics perspective, creating prescribing issues for physicians and safety issues for patients.  The concerns with this prescriptive approach are that it would not only hinder appropriate management of the opioid-tolerant patient s pain but could also result in safety issues due to patient confusion and the potential for medication errors when multiple tablet strengths were required to achieve a prescribed dose.  There is also the additional safety concern for patients attempting to split tablets to save money on the additional strength prescriptions.

 

This prescriptive approach is especially concerning combined with the removal of the proposed 25% dose reduction from previous opioid therapy, which was based on the EXALGO clinical trial (50% reductions were never studied).  Drastic dose reductions in this opioid tolerant population could lead to repeat, i.e., over-dosing due to inadequacy of the first dose and the 4 days that are required to achieve steady state for EXALGO.  Similarly, the minimal 4-mg dose increment could increase the rates of withdrawal symptoms in the opioid-tolerant patients who would be prescribed EXALGO.

 

Mallinckrodt recommends initiation at 8, 12, 16, 24, or 32 mg followed by an 8-mg titrating dose for EXALGO until stabilized. 

 

Thank you for your efforts to finalize this class labeling for EXALGO.

Kind regards,

Linda

Hi Linda, Here is the amended PI for Exalgo.  Please accept the changes and return to me via email ASAP but no later than COB Thursday.  Once we are sure it is absolutely final, I will instruct you to formally submit. 

 

In addition, please correct the left margin Recent Major Changes lines so that they do not indent with the text.

 

Thanks!

 

Lisa E. Basham, M.S.

Senior Regulatory Health Project Manager

Division of Anesthesia, Analgesia, and Addiction Products

Office of Drug Evaluation II

Center for Drug Evaluation and Research

301-796-1175

lisa.basham@fda.hhs.gov


 



-----
 The 4?mg dose increment is problematic from a prescription/patient instructions-logistics perspective, creating prescribing issues for physicians and safety issues for patients.  The concerns with this prescriptive approach are that it would not only hinder appropriate management of the opioid-tolerant patient s pain but could also result in safety issues due to patient confusion and the potential for medication errors when multiple tablet strengths were required to achieve a prescribed dose.  There is also the additional safety concern for patients attempting to split tablets to save money on the additional strength prescriptions. 

This prescriptive approach is especially concerning combined with the removal of the proposed 25% dose reduction from previous opioid therapy, which was based on the EXALGO clinical trial (50% reductions were never studied).  Drastic dose reductions in this opioid tolerant population could lead to repeat, i.e., over-dosing due to inadequacy of the first dose and the 4 days that are required to achieve steady state for EXALGO.  Similarly, the minimal 4-mg dose increment could increase the rates of withdrawal symptoms in the opioid-tolerant patients who would be prescribed EXALGO. 

Mallinckrodt recommends initiation at 8, 12, 16, 24 or 32 mg followed by an 8-mg titrating dose for EXALGO until stabilized. 



 Note to Sponsor:  include increments in mg. for increases

David, Jane and Ginger -

We have completed our quarterly SOM review of the two "Top 20" lists with McKesson's Southern Region.  We have also completed the same exercise with ABC's lists except for several open items.  In that process, we have identified pharmacies that are exhibiting signs indicative of diversion.  We have also learned of some recent pharmacy raids by DEA and we are including those pharmacies in the letter as well. We are ready to send out a letter to the distributors informing them that effective immediately, we will not be processing charge backs for sales of our products to certain pharmacies.

The blocked pharmacies are listed below.  I have included the key points related to each.  Please note that the SOM Leadership Team based its decision to block the pharmacies on a number of other facts in addition to the key points noted.

ACCOKEEK DRUG HEALTHCARE, INC.
15789 LIVINGSTON RD.
ACCOKEEK,MD 20607
DEA. No. BA6800216
McKesson informed us that during a pharmacy due diligence on-site visit, wholesaler identified seven prescriptions from one physician for extremely large amounts of oxycodone that were filled on sequentially numbered prescriptions.  McKesson has blocked this account.

LAABS INC.
911 NORTH 27 STREET
MILWAUKEE, WI 53208
DEA No. AL3934014
McKesson informed us that pharmacy raided by DEA and Milwaukee police, which we confirmed by reviewing local media article.  McKesson has blocked this account.

LIFE PHARMA II INC.
471 LENOX AVE
NEW YORK, NY 10037
DEA No. FL1001077
McKesson informed us that pharmacy was ordering over 75% oxycodone 30 mg dosage units as compared to all other oxycodone SKUs purchased.  McKesson's SOM due diligence review included obtaining a listing of the pharmacy's highest oxycodone 30 mg prescribing physicians.  Three doctors were writing over 50% of the oxycodone 30 mg prescriptions filled at the pharmacy.  Those doctors' offices are located in Brooklyn, Queens, Bronx, whereas the pharmacy is located Harlem.  McKesson has blocked this account.

MOBLEY'S DISCOUNT PHARMACY, INC.
235 WEST WARD STREET
DOUGLAS, GA   31533
DEA No. BM4332134

and

SAVMORX DRUGS
205 EAST OCMULGEE STREET
BROXTON, GA   31519
DEA No. FS1757701
From National Association of Drug Diversion Investigators (NADDI) RxNews Report dated 02/06/12:  A father and son who operate these two drug stores in GA were both arrested for selling prescription drugs to people who did not have prescriptions.  The pharmacy locations were raided by DEA agents.

Attached are:


(1)   the form of letter with the list of distributors to whom the letter will be sent, and

(2)   and recent chargeback activity with respect to the pharmacies.

The letters will go out today by FedEx and will be bcc'd to Don Lohman, Bill Ratliff, Gail Tetzlaff, Ginger Collier, Jane Williams, Scott Parker and Lisa Cardetti.

I am okay with the NAMs or Jane sending the letter to their counterparts at the various distributors tomorrow so they have a heads up.  Under separate cover to Jane, Chris Inman will be sending separate .pdfs for each of the letters so Jane can send the correct letters to the correct NAMs for transmission to their counterparts, if that is what Jane wants to do.

Jane - In your email to your direct reports with the letter, please include language like the following:

"The attached letters have been generated as part of our Suspicious Order Monitoring Program.  If customers have any questions concerning this letter, please have them contact Karen Harper, Senior Manager, Controlled Substance Compliance at (314) 654-1868."

I will be sending the letters by .pdf to our SOM counterparts at Cardinal, McKesson, ABC, H.D. Smith, Smith Drug, Anda and Quest as well.

As always, please contact me with any questions.
Donald A. Lohman

Megan,

 

Here are the changes for page 5 and 7.  Thanks, Carol

 Page 5 on the left side, I am combining the 2 sections:

Dealing with pain while  EXALGOTM is reaching effective levels

EXALGO is an extended-release medication.  It usually takes 6 to 8 hours for you to begin to feel pain relief.  Since the active ingredient (hydromorphone) in EXALGO is slowly released into the bloodstream, it may take up to 3-4 days for EXALGO to reach maximum effectiveness.  At that point, the medicine in EXALGO should remain at a constant and effective level.  Your doctor will help you manage any pain during this time.  Do not take another dose of EXALGO within 24 hours unless your doctor tells you.  Taking a second dose within 24 hours may cause you to overdose. An overdose can cause death.

Page 7 on the left side under

Only take EXALGO if . . .

You have moderate to severe chronic pain.
You have been taking an opioid medicine up until the time you were prescribed EXALGO, so your body is used to taking these medicines.
You need to be on a pain relief medicine for a long time. Ask your doctor if you are unsure you are taking an opioid medicine.

Don't take EXALGO if...

  You  need management of mild pain or pain that is not expected to continue for a long time

  You are having an asthma attack or have severe asthma, trouble breathing, or certain other lung problems

  You have narrowing  of the stomach or intestines or have bowel blockage

  You have a history of surgery in your stomach or intestines.

  You are allergic to any of the ingredients in EXALGO, including hydromorphone or sulfites. 

  You are taking a monoamine oxidase inhibitor medicine (MAOI)

 

On the right side under

Before taking EXALGOTM, tell your doctor . . .

  You are pregnant or planning to become pregnant

   If you will be or are taking other medicines. Other medicines include prescription and nonprescription drugs, vitamins, and herbal supplements.

  About all of your medical and/or mental problems, especially the ones listed below:

  Trouble breathing or lung problems, such as asthma, wheezing, or shortness of breath

  A head injury

  Liver or kidney problems

  Seizures (convulsions or fits)

  Low blood pressure

  Mental problems, including major depression, anxiety, and hallucinations (seeing or hearing things that are not there)

  Drinking problem, alcoholism, or a family history of these problems

  Past or present drug abuse, addiction problem, or a family history of these problems

> Hi Tina,
> 
>      I hope that you are doing well:) I have a question that was brought to my attention from a physician yesterday as an objection. I think that I handled it as best as could be although he was still somewhat questioning. I thought that he was sending out a " smokescreen" until someone else brought it up..Today a PA called me due to a patient's XR script having to be switched due to the patient's concern over the same issue.. On our coupons and literature there is a very pronounced disclaimer regarding risk of abuse, death etc.. This is language that patient's and HCPs are familiar with regarding opioids.. What is articulated a little different that " put off" the physician and now patient is the language regarding how death can occur even if taken as prescribed and after other medicines basically are not adequate.. I understand what this means as someone can obviously die even if taking as prescribed due to various other variables.. Also I and most HCPs understand that an acute opioid is generally written after or when an NSAID etc will not suffice. The language though is strung together in a way though that HCPs have not seen with other opioids.. As for the patient the PA and physician "broke it all down" for them but the death even if taken as prescribed scared them.. I looked at all opioid leave behinds/ coupons as well as Zohydro's warnings and disclaimers and could not find anything like. They were all similar to Exalgo which breaks down for ex why risk of death or abuse.. I am just curious and would like feedback if this comes up again as to why our wording is a little different.. Although  it is saying the same thing as others it is in a more succinct and different manner that can be perceived as, " I risk dying if taking this even as prescribed and it should be last resort". My HCP thought that the language made him appear more liable if someone abuses etc and at a detriment if ever sued because it states clearly that can die and use other medicines first. I get it but what is the reason that our language is "different".. ? I know that they have " tightened" up on opioid labeling but again ours is unique.Sorry if provided too much info. Hopefully it makes sense.. Thanks so much!
> 
> Rachel

	Pharmacy to Pay $250,000 to Settle Federal Civil Charges
	SEP 10 --  (Manhattan, NY) JOHN P. GILBRIDE, the Special Agent-in-Charge of
	the New York  Office of the United States Drug Enforcement Administration
	("DEA"), MICHAEL J.  GARCIA, the United States Attorney for the Southern District
	of New York  announced yesterday that a Manhattan pharmacy -- THIRD AVENUE
	PHARMACY &  SURGICALS, INC. ( THIRD AVENUE PHARMACY ) -- and its owner, IRA KARP,
	have  agreed to pay $250,000 to resolve civil charges that: the pharmacy
	filled  prescriptions obtained through the Internet outside the course of a
	legitimate  physician-patient relationship; some of these prescriptions were filled
	by  employees who were not registered pharmacists; the pharmacy failed to
	maintain  accurate records on these prescriptions.
	The settlement agreement  was filed simultaneously with the Complaint on
	September 5, 2008. United States  District Court Judge P. KEVIN CASTEL approved
	the settlement yesterday in  Manhattan federal court. According to the charges
	alleged in the Complaint filed  by the United States in this case:
	From November 2005 until  June 2006, THIRD AVENUE PHARMACY, under the
	direction of IRA KARP, filled at  least 6,298 invalid prescriptions received from
	approximately 70 different  websites selling controlled substances to members of
	the public without valid  prescriptions. The business or businesses operating
	these websites employed a  small number of physicians who were paid to
	authorize prescriptions on demand  for various appetite suppressants and sleeping
	pills - all of which were  Schedule III or Schedule IV controlled substances --
	without any medical  examination of the customers seeking the prescriptions.
	The prescriptions  that
	THIRD AVENUE PHARMACY  received from these websites each contained the name
	and address of the  physician authorizing the prescription and the name and
	address of the customer  requesting the prescription. The physicians  addresses
	bore no relation to the  customers  addresses, which were scattered across the
	United States   clearly  indicating that the customers were not patients of
	and had not been examined by  the authorizing physicians. Accordingly, IRA KARP
	and THIRD AVENUE PHARMACY  knowingly dispensed controlled substances in the
	absence of a valid  prescription, in violation of the Controlled Substances Act.
	Some or all of these  invalid prescriptions were filled, at the direction of
	IRA KARP, by THIRD AVENUE  PHARMACY employees who were not licensed
	pharmacists, and THIRD AVENUE PHARMACY  failed to maintain accurate records of the
	prescriptions. Both of these  practices constitute separate violations of the
	Controlled Substances Act also  charged in the Complaint.
	The settlement of the  Complaint requires IRA KARP and THIRD AVENUE PHARMACY
	to pay $250,000 in civil  penalties and prohibits THIRD AVENUE PHARMACY from
	filling any prescriptions in  the future outside of its walk-in business. THIRD
	AVENUE PHARMACY and IRA KARP  did not admit any wrongdoing.
	Mr. GARCIA praised the  efforts of the Drug Enforcement Administration,
	Diversion Group D-62 for its  investigative work in this matter.
	Assistant United States  Attorney SERRIN TURNER is in charge of the case.

One other thing stands out in this story - what the physician/staff did NOT know about Pennsaid. We had a good sale rep there prior to Matt. I'm fairly certain that she told them all of these things before. But still they didn't KNOW. That's probably why we topped out at 8 scripts. Team,

I had to share this organic success story from Matt Goddard out of Charleston, SC!

Another example on our team of appropriate targeting, irrepressible enthusiasm and drive!!!

As I've already shared, my mantra.....Define your path!

Excellent Matt!

Begin forwarded message:
From: "Goddard, Matthew S" <Matthew.Goddard@covidien.com<mailto:Matthew.Goddard@covidien.com>>
Date: August 30, 2011 11:00:49 PM EDT
To: "Dean, Todd E" <Todd.Dean@covidien.com<mailto:Todd.Dean@covidien.com>>
Subject: Success
Todd,

I just wanted to share a success that I had today with a Doctor.  It has the potential to boost my sales through the roof and I am excited to see where this relationship can go.

I had a lunch today with Dr. John Demarco of Palmetto Orthopaedics.  The practice has 4 physicians and they have 2 offices in the Charleston area.  He is the #1 Voltaren Gel writer in my territory.  He has a total market basket of 644 and 333 of them are Voltaren Gel......... 52% market share.  2 of the other physicians are also in my top 6 writers of Voltaren Gel.  They each have a market share of 59% and 20% respectively with V Gel.  So, as you can see, a huge opportunity for Pennsaid in this practice, especially since between the 3 of them they have written a grand total of......wait for it....... 8!!!! 8 scripts out of 1700.  C'mon man!!!

Back to my lunch, I went in with a "sponge approach", played the new card,  and just wanted to learn as much as I could about his practice and his state of mind.  I asked a lot of questions about topicals, why Voltaren Gel, what's the difference between a Pennsaid patient and a VG patient, what pharmacy they refer to,  etc.  I got a lot of information from him and his staff and then I switched roles and told  him and his staff that they must have questions for me and then I let them ask me questions.  It worked great.

I spent 45 minutes with him, his staff, and his assistant and answered every question they had.

*         Dosing - didn't understand how easy it was; didn't know how to write it;

*         Didn't really know why he wrote VGel- it was first, but no real loyalty is what he said; didn't even know VGel reps names

*         Samples are huge - no samples=no scripts; Co-pay cards, knee models, patient ed., they wanted it all

*         Has never seen study about Physical function being measured

*         Didn't know about lotions, suntan lotion, insect repellent, etc. and no use with VGel; never been told that;

*         Formulary and pharmacy questions; price questions; Medicare Part D;

I then ended the call with one question and said what can I do to become a resource and earn more of your business?  He said just keep him in the loop, remind him of Pennsaid dosing, work with Danielle on samples and managed care questions and he will use Pennsaid.  He also said that he will talk with the other MD's about Pennsaid and recommend that they try it as well.   I gave him my card with my cell and email, told him he can call me with anything and then he gave me his cell number as well.

In closing, this was a great day and I definitely feel like I sold something today.  I'm going to stay in front of this office and follow up with him on Tuesday next week to see how things have progressed and what else I can do.  I've been doing this for a long time and I know not everyday is going to be this way, but man it felt good to have a possible score with this physician and office.

Hope this helps and I'll talk with you soon.

Thanks,

Matt Goddard
Covidien Specialty Pharmaceuticals
Field Sales Specialist
Charleston, SC
Cell: 843-754-1237
"Nothing great was ever achieved without enthusiasm." - Ralph Waldo Emerson

Subject: RAGA Weekly Recap April 1-7, 2017
From: RAGA Weekly Newsletter <info@republicanags.com>
Date: Fri, 07 Apr 2017 17:28:01 +0000
To: Derek Naten <derek.naten@mallinckrodt.com>



No Images? Click here






Friday, April 7, 2017

Weekly Newsletter

RAGA Weekly Recap

April 1-7, 2017





 
POLITICAL NEWS


VIRGINIA: Adams certified as the GOP nominee for AG, vows to restore the rule of law to the office: Late last week, the Republican Party of Virginia announced John Adams to be the only Republican candidate for attorney general to qualify for the June 13th Primary ballot. Adams, who now is able to focus all his efforts on Democratic Attorney General Mark Herring in the November General Election, delivered the weekly Virginia GOP address, in which he called for the office to return to upholding the rule of law. “When I am your Attorney General, I will restore the office to its proper role as a law firm for the Commonwealth,” said Adams. “It will be an office that respects the will of the people, and defends the laws the people pass through their elected representatives. It will be an office that provides fair, consistent, and objective legal advice to all government officials throughout the Commonwealth, regardless of whether they are Democrats or Republicans. It will be an office that stands for true equality in the enforcement of our laws, and a robust defense of the rule of law.” Adams is a former Naval officer, federal prosecutor, White House lawyer under President George W. Bush and clerk to U.S. Supreme Court Justice Clarence Thomas.

Adams also released his first campaign advertisement, "Just Getting Started," that introduces Adams and his family to Virginians, why he is running and his priorities as the Commonwealth's next top law enforcement officer. 






NEW HAMPSHIRE: MacDonald unanimously confirmed as state AG: This week the five-member Executive Council voted unanimously to confirm Republican Governor Chris Sununu’s nominee, Manchester attorney Gordon MacDonald, to serve as the state’s 30th attorney general. The Council, made up of three Republicans and two Democrats, cited no opposition at last week’s public hearing on MacDonald’s nomination. After the vote, MacDonald said he was looking forward to getting to work. "I’m looking forward to diving in and doing all I can for the people of New Hampshire,” said MacDonald. 


 

POLICY UPDATE


FLORIDA: Combatting opioid abuse will take a united front, writes Attorney General Bondi in op-ed: Following her appointment to the President’s Opioid and Drug Abuse Commission, Attorney General Pam Bondi authored an op-ed in the Sun Sentinel about taking on the opioid epidemic in our country. “I fought to bring together law enforcement, lawmakers and public health leaders. We passed legislation banning doctor shopping, implemented a prescription drug monitoring database and ultimately shutdown pain clinics handing out painkillers like candy,” wrote AG Bondi. Florida was previously known as the pill mill capital of the country with 98 of the top 100 oxycodone dispensers residing there. Attorney General Bondi has also partnered with the DEA and local law enforcement to tackle drug traffickers shipping opioids and heroin across the state. She continues, “One dose of these dangerous opioid cocktails can kill instantly. That is why Florida law enforcement alone cannot stop this national epidemic and I am deeply encouraged by President Donald Trump's creation of the Opioid and Drug Abuse Commission.”

LOUISIANA: Attorney General Landry helps to launch opioid public awareness campaign: A new effort to increase public awareness of the growing opioid epidemic was launched this week by Attorney General Jeff Landry and partners in the private sector. The “End the Epidemic” campaign includes a website with resources for those looking for more information on opioid abuse and how to spot it, as well as advertisements and other public outreach efforts. “From the big cities to our rural towns, no community in Louisiana is immune to the opioid abuse epidemic,” Attorney General Landry said in a statement. “Opioid abuse has taken the lives of too many of our children, parents, neighbors, and co-workers. We hope that End the Epidemic LA will assist in the reduction of opioid misuse, abuse, and overdose.” Last year New Orleans saw overdose deaths outpace those from homicide for the first time in the city’s history. Louisiana is also one of eight states where there are more opioid prescriptions than residents.

 LOUISIANA: Attorney General Landry speaks out against sanctuary city policies: Following US Attorney General Jeff Sessions’ announcement that sanctuary cities risk federal funding, Louisiana Attorney General Jeff Landry voiced his support for the administration’s move. “This is not a time for politics; it is time for leaders to work together to solve this evident public safety issue. And I applaud Attorney General Sessions and the Trump administration for taking the correct steps to order cities to follow federal law,” said Attorney General Landry. Attorney General Sessions’ announcement comes after President Trump’s executive order in January that directed the Departments of Homeland Security and Justice to withhold federal funds from sanctuary cities. AG Landry has been critical of New Orleans’ lack of cooperation with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement, the only sanctuary city located in the state. “We have an illegal immigration problem across the country and certainly in Louisiana. Unfortunately, New Orleans is part of this problem as the only Sanctuary City in Louisiana,” said Landry.

MISSOURI: Attorney General Hawley announces new actions to combat human trafficking: On Monday, Attorney General Josh Hawley announced several new initiatives his office is taking to combat human trafficking in Missouri. A new anti-trafficking unit will be created within the Attorney General’s office, composed of prosecutors and investigators who will enforce new regulations that have been issued and provide aid to local prosecutors. Regulations include the prohibition of debt bondage and the establishment of a business as a front for a trafficking operation. “I became a lawyer because I believe in justice, and justice means protecting the vulnerable and the exploited. I am proud to announce these efforts to make Missouri a leader in the fight to abolish trafficking. To the criminals who would exploit the weak, the vulnerable and the oppressed, I say this: Missouri is officially closed for your kind of business,” said Attorney Josh Hawley.

Subject: EXALGO Monitoring Report -- Week of 5/21



 

Hi team,

 

Below please find this week s monitoring report for EXALGO; this report includes coverage from Friday, May 14, to Friday, May 21, 2010.

 

This week, RecoveryView.com published an editorial about EXALGO, citing its concerns for the potential abuse and misuse of the medication. The article begins by highlighting the evolution in pain management from Oxycontin, a 12-hour formula for pain management, to EXALGO, which is taken every 24 hours. The reporter s concerns with the drug is that opiate-na ve patients are at high-risk for overdosing on EXALGO, and that there may be a greater possibility for people to divert the drug for illegal sale. The reporter did have hope that, with proper patient and prescriber education, the drug will be used to effectively treat opioid-tolerant patients who suffer from moderate to severe chronic pain.

 

Of other interest this week: A conversation about EXALGO was posted on the CafePharma forum titled,  Five reasons why EXALGO ER is a failure.  The forum post highlighted the top-five reasons one member felt EXALGO was not going to be successful, including the price of the medication and the potential risks involved with taking EXALGO. One person replied to the forum claiming to be a representative from Covidien, accusing the person who began the discussion of being an employee of a competitor.

 

The Los Angeles Times wrote a blog post this week about an essay published in the past issue of the Journal of the American Medical Association (JAMA). The essay was written by a medical researcher who made headlines last year when his fianc e died after the two injected themselves with a narcotic buprenorphine. The author of the essay became addicted to opioids, marijuana and other drugs while studying the effects of drugs on the brain for the University of Maryland. The author is quoted in the blog post as saying that,   when it comes to drug use, the perception of control is really nothing more than an illusion. 

 

Finally, Fierce Pharma Manufacturing posted an article this week that listed tips on creating a successful REMS program. The article highlighted three tips from REMS experts on making a successful program: start creating your REMS program early, do your user and product homework, engage your users and stockholders to line up potential resources.

 

Attached please find the full-text coverage. As always, please let us know if you have any questions.

 

Thanks,

Cari
